subtopic: FINANCIAL TERMS BETWEEN CANADA AND NOVA SCOTIA.

speechtext:
Mr. BELL-by Mr. Taylor-asked :
1.	How often and at what dates were financial terms arranged between the Dominion of Canada and the province of Nova Scotia, between January 1, 1872, and July 1, 1896 ?
2.	By what amount was the sum payable to Nova Scotia increased by these different arrangements ?
3.	What sum is at present at credit of the government of Nova Scotia, bearing interest, with the government of Canada ?

subtopic: FINANCIAL TERMS BETWEEN CANADA AND NOVA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
No financial terms were arranged between the Dominion of Canada and the province of Nova Scotia between the dates mentioned. There were general readjustments in 1873 and 1884 of the debt accounts of the various provinces, but they had no special relation to Nova Scotia.
3.	The sum now at the credit of Nova Scotia in the debt account is $1,056,111.12.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: Is it the intention of the government to take part in the St. Louis International Exhibition in 1904 ? If so, will the Canadian commissioners be simply attaches to the British commission, as in Paris in 1900 ; or will they be given all the lights and privileges of an independent national commission, such as were granted to Canada at the Philadelphia International Exhibition of 1876 ?

It is the intention of the government to take part in the St. Louis International Exhibition in 1904.
The Canadian commissioner or commissioners who may be appointed will not be attaches to the British commission, but will be independent of it. The rights and privileges of the Canadian commission have not yet been determined.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext:
That a Select Committee, composed of Messrs. Charlton, Casgrain, Russell, Barker, Demers (St. John and Iberville), Northrup, Thompson (Haldimand), and Ingram, and the mover, be appointed to consider the state of the laws respecting Dominion elections ; with power to report from time to time. And that the order respecting Bill No. 3, intituled : ' An Act to amend the Dominion Elections Act, 1900,' be discharged ; and that the said Bill be referred to the said committee.
He said : Mr. Speaker, at an earlier stage in the session a discussion arose on the election law in connection with a Bill introduced by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). In the course of that discussion I ventured to suggest that if any good could be accomplished in the way of improving the election law, it might be possible to bring it about by the appointment of a committee representing both sides of the House which would study the subject and which would probably then be able to make a report to the House. That suggestion found general favour, and after consultation with the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) I placed this motion on the notice paper. I am by no means too confident that we can reform all the evils which are sometimes mentioned in connection with elections. I am afraid that some of them lie more deeply than legislation, and that in respect to some of them we would have to reform human nature before we could entirely remove them. However, I think that no harm could possibly result but that some good may come of the study of this question by a joint committee in the manner suggested. Therefore without further words, i beg to move that a committee be appointed for the purpose named. I move the motion which stands in my name.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding) moved :

speechtext: Would the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) be good enough to tell us whether this inquiry will involve the duty of looking into the conduct of elections, the actions of officers connected with elections and offences committed during elections ?
I do not understand that the committee will undertake to look into any election that is past.
I mean the law.
Yes, anything which will help to improve the election law would, I think, come under the view of the committee.

The point I wish to make is this : At the present time only the deputy returning officer is allowed to place his initial upon, or to touch the ballot which is handed to the voter. It was my intention to bring in a Bill to deal with this subject, but when I saw that another lion, member had a Bill before the House, I thought that I would have an opportunity to offer an amendment. I think that not only the deputy returning officer should initial the ballot, but that the agent of the candidate should also be allowed to place any distinctive mark he chooses in proper form on the stub of the ballot, so that it may be identified. Would that point be eligible to be brought before the committee ?
Yes. in my judgment, it would. That is our intention.

I presume the intention of this motion is to lay before this committee all the laws at present relating to the conduct of Dominion elections, and those that are intended to deal with irregularities at elections. It will, I presume, involve the introduction of a new Bill, although I observe that Bill No. 3, introduced by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), is referred to a special committee for consideration. I would suppose that the intention is to review all the legislation * now in existence in Canada in reference to the conducting of elections and in reference to irregularities or wrongs done at elections, with the view of introducing a Bill that will cover the ground and probably of substituting some more efficient legislation than that which we now have.

That would be our desire, and certainly all these matters will come within the authority of the committee, and if they should be able to reach a conclusion that would, I should think, be in the shape of a Bill to be submitted to the House. Certainly what the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) has suggested would come within the scope of the inquiry.
I suppose that would include the Election Act as well as the Controverted Elections Act.
I do not see why we should not include both.
And no doubt it would also include the introduction of some measures which are altogether new-for instance, compulsory voting.
It might be so. The committee would have a free hand.
Motion agreed to.

House went into committee on the following proposed resolution :
That it is expedient to repeal section 1 of chapter 9 pf the statutes of 1899, and enact, in lieu thereof, the following section :-
If any company or body corporate, approved by the Governor in Council, as having the ability to perform the work, enters into an agreement with His Majesty to construct a dry dock, with all proper and necessary equipment, machinery and plant, for the reception and repairing of vessels, at a place, and according to plans and specifications approved by the Governor in Council, on a report by the Minister of Public Works, as sufficient for the requirements of the public at such place ; the work to be completed within a time to be limited by

such agreement. Then, provided the company performs the work according to such agreement. and to the satisfaction of the Minister of Public Works, under the supervision of whose department the work shall be done, the Governor in Council may authorize the payment out of any unappropriated moneys forming part of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, of a subsidy not exceeding three per cent per annum on the cost of the work during twenty years from the time of its completion and acceptance by the said minister ; provided that such subsidy shall not exceed thirty thousand dollars per annum ; and that the cost on which it shall be calculated shall not be greater than the value of the work as estimated by the said minister. Provided also, that the subsidy shall not be payable for any portion of the said twenty years during which the dock is not in complete repair and working order.-The Minister of Finance.

This resolution proposes to amend an Act which has been on the statute-book for several years. Some years ago the government constructed some docks as government works, but apart from that an Act was placed on the statute-book making provision for grants by way of aid to incorporated companies which might construct docks of the proper character subject to the approval of the government. The original arrangement was that that aid might take the shape of a subsidy equal to 2 per cent on the cost of the dock, for a period of twenty years, not exceeding, however, in any case, $10,000 per annum, which would be 2 per cent upon $500,000. That was the state of the law for some time. In the year 1899, an amendment was made whereby we still retained the 2 per cent, but we enlarged the amount upon which the payment might be made in order that docks of a larger capacity might be constructed. The Act as it now stands makes provision for payments of 2 per cent upon the cost of the dock, not exceeding, however, $20,000 per annum. The change which we now propose is to make the rate which we may pay by way of subsidy, 3 per cent instead of 2 per cent, and with a corresponding change in the total amount-instead of 2 per cent, or $20,000 we may pay in the case stated, 3 per cent, or $30,000 per annum. The change is entirely with respect to the rate per cent. It has been found that some difficulty has been experienced in floating companies to build these docks upon the present basis, and it is represented to us that if this increase be made, docks would be constructed in some places where otherwise they might not be. The only dock constructed under the old Act was the one at Halifax which was constructed by the joint aid of the imperial, the Dominion and the city governments. The city of Halifax paid a certain sum per annum, the Dominion government a certain sum per annum, and the imperial government gave a subsidy in consideration of which the ships of His Majesty's navy were received into the dock. There is a dock proposed and some progress has been made on it at Collingwood, Ontario, which no doubt would come in under the operation of this Act. They have been negotiating, and a contract was made on the basis of the present Act, but I think not much progress has been made, and I suppose the Collingwood Company would expect to avail themselves of the advantages of this Act. Another dock which has been brought to our notice is at the port of St. John, N.B., where it is represented that with this increased aid, the company will be able to establish a dock of a large character adapted to the increasing trade of the port. The policy of all governments in times past having been to aid works of this character, the only question is one of proportion, and inasmuch as 2 per cent has not been found a sufficient sum to bring about the construction of any docks in recent years, it is proposed to enlarge the aid by granting 3 per cent; with the maximum of $30,000 per annum for a period of twenty years.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: Have any companies, except that at Collingwood, applied for the aid provided for by this resolution ?

I think I am correct in saying that no application has been made by any other company. Occasionally mention has been made of projects in other quarters, but I think I am right in saying that no application has been made by any company except the company at St. John and the company at Collingwood.
Of course the plans will be submitted in the usual way for approval by the government.
There is no change whatever in the words of the Act in that respect.

Is it contemplated that the government itself will not in future build any dry docks ? I speak of this, because for a long time we had expected that the government would construct a dry dock in the vicinity of the port of Montreal. Would we be met by the objection, that now that this system has been inaugurated it would be incumbent upon some private parties to organize themselves into a dock company in order to come under the provisions of this resolution ; or, would the government still persist in what has been promised to the port of Montreal, and build a dry dock there ?

I must not discuss the question of any promise to any particular port; but under this Act any body corporate, which would include the Harbour Commissioners, if they should see fit, could come in and obtain the benefits of this Act. Whether or not the government will in any case or in no case build or not build a dock in the future ; that is too definite a question for me to answer. In the present instance, the wording of the

Act is such that if the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal desire to come in under the operations of this Act, they would receive the aid. As to whether or not the government will in that case, or in other cases undertake the construction of the work as a government dock, that is a matter that would have to be considered hereafter. I am not at present able to say anything more definite.

This is not a new policy at all. It is simply the extension in a small way of the existing policy which has been in force for over twenty years. The inference which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) fears may possibly be drawn from this Bill, is an inference that could as well be drawn from any previous Bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I should have added that though the resolution before the House only deals, as the parliamentary rules require, with the money side of the question ; in the Bill to be founded thereon, provision will be made that the tolls to be charged on any dock to be constructed hereafter shall be subject to the approval of the Governor General in Council. That has not been so in the past, but that restriction will be placed upon any docks constructed hereafter under the terms of this Act.
Mi-. BENNETT. In considering an application to aid in the construction of a dock under this Act, would the first consideration be that there would have to be a certain amount expended for the work to be constructed ?

We have made no rule in that regard. We have rather taken for granted that docks of large size would be undertaken. The only limit is that we shall only pay the 3 per cent on the fair cost of construction ; and though the cost may be very much larger than the limit fixed, the amount of the subsidy cannot exceed $30,000. In the case of the Halifax dock the cost was very much larger than the estimated cost on which the government subsidy was paid.

I do not say that private enterprise must not be encouraged in cases of this kind. I think that what has suggested the present Bill is the case of the dock at St. John, N.B. Some very energetic citizens took up the proposal to erect a dock there. I understand that they received some encouragement or had some hopes of aid from the imperial government. Those hopes did not materialize. If I am not mistaken, they also received some help from the provincial government and from the city of St. John ; but they could not get along without some further help. I quite agree with my hon. friends that the measure before the House to-day is worthy of ap-Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
proval. I may say also that the dock at Collingwood is being built by very energetic men. But we must not rely too much on private enterprise in large transactions of this kind. There is no country in the world which is more lacking in dock accommodation than Canada. The United States have many small docks, but they have not one large dock. During the last season there were in the St. Lawrence at one time four or five large ships which suffered damages and could not get accommodation either at Montreal or elsewhere. Suppose an accident happened between Belle Isle and Quebec ; there is only one dock at Quebec, and one at Montreal, a very small one, belonging to a private firm. 1 would call the attention of my hon. friends on the treasury benches to the great importance of equipping our harbours with this necessary improvement. Graving docks are essential to-day, and they will become more and more essential as. our fleet increases in size and number.
What about the dock at L6vis ?

The dock at L6vis can only accommodate one ship at a time, and it is too narrow for the largest ships that ply in our waters. The boards of trade of Montreal and Quebec have applied for a second dock at Levis. We should also have one at Montreal. I only say these few words in passing, in order to call the attention of my hon. friends to this important question.

While I do not propose to offer any objection to the resolution, per-ferring to wait until the Bill is brought down, it seems to me, on the face of the resolution, that unless the Bill goes further, a great deal of difficulty will arise. Since the case of the Collingwood dock has been instanced, let me call the minister's attention to the fact that there is also a dock at Owen Sound. I think the Collingwood dock was originally larger than the one at Owen Sound ; but if this Bill goes into effect, the people of Owen Sound will no doubt come and ask that the dock there which has been enlarged at the expense of the company who own it, probably with the aid of the town, be assisted by the government. To my mind the government should lay down a hard and fast principle as a starting point, to the effect that the docks to be subsidized shall be placed at a certain distance from each other, or that only one dock shall be aided in a particular water. I am not in a position to state what was the original cost of the Collingwood dock ; but unless a very large amount is expended in improving and enlarging it, it seems to me that $30,000 will be a very large grant towards it. Under the wording of the resolution, the $30,000 might be a greater inducement to the company than 3 per cent of the amount invested.
But they can only get 3 per cent on the cost of the dock, and In any case the amount must not exceed $30,000.

I did not notice that it was optional. When the Bill comes down, I think there should be some provision inserted in it as to the size of docks to he aided and the distance that they must be from each other. Otherwise assistance will be asked for very small docks, and the result will be a multiplicity of small docks instead of the establishment of a few large ones.
Did the hon. minister say that if this Bill becomes law, it will apply to the Collingwood dock ?

What I said was that I supposed the Collingwood company would expect to come under this Act in the same way as the company which built the dock at St. John. As not much progress has been made with the work at Colingwood
Oh, yes.
The dock has been there for twenty years.
But I understand that the whole dock is to be reconstructed.

As I read the resolution, the aid is to be granted towards the construction of new docks, but not towards the enlargement or improvement of existing docks. I would like to know from the minister what the intention is in that respect ?

If the Collingwood dock in its original construction had been subsidized by the government, then anything done later would be an enlargement ; but as it did not receive any government aid in its original form, all the work done on it now is practically new construction. I understand that there is none of the small original dock remaining, but that the whole dock is being reconstructed ; and, as in the first place it received no government aid, it will be treated as an entirely new construction.
The old dock at Collingwood was simply a hole and nothing else.

I understood the hon. minister to say that this is simply in pursuance of a policy inaugurated a number of years ago, and that the only change was an increase in the percentage from two to three. Might I ask whether under the Order in Council or statutory law, there is a condition precedent that the dock to be constructed should cost a certain amount ?

There is not any such condition, but the plans 95
have to be submitted to the Minister of Public Works and by him to the Governor General in Council for approval. Whether there should be any amount fixed may be a matter for consideration, but we are simply following the policy laid down in the Act in times past.
I notice that the Act was first passed in 1899, so that it must have been passed during the hon. gentleman's term of office. Have any companies taken advantage of the two per cent clause ?
The Act of 1899 was an amendment. The original Act was passed many years before.

I think that we should encourage the building of dry docks, but under the provision of this resolution, it will be in the power of the government to grant very large amounts of public money without the special authorization of parliament. I would invite my hon. friend to consider that point when framing his Bill. For instance, when this resolution becomes law, the government will be empowered to grant over $2,000,000 of public money without the special authority of parliament- $30,000 a year for twenty years. And as the construction of these docks may become frequent, although we are proceeding on a law which has been in force a number of years, I think that it is worthy of consideration whether it is prudent to give such a very large power of disposing of public funds to the Governor General in Council.

The best answer to my bon. friend is that this Act, in one form or other, has been on the statute since 1882, and up to the present we have only subsidized one dock under it. We may, therefore, conclude that the difficulty surrounding the construction and carrying on of large enterprises of that character will always impose certain checks on the demand for public aid, although, of course, by this amendment, we are making temptation stronger than it was in the past.

In my opinion the trouble will be that the percentage proposed, is not high enough, because these docks have not hitherto been paying investments by any means. The percentage is not sufficient inducement for capitalists to put money into such enterprises, and, I think, that the government might very well make it much higher.

My hon. friend's criticism has something in it. It shows that the risk involved is a protection against any excessive payments under the Act. But I hope that the increase from two to three per cent will lead to the construction of one or two docks. The Collingwood dock will be finished and we will probably have one at St. John. Possibly other applications may come forward, and if there are sections where such accommoda-

[DOT]son

tion is needed, we shall not regret supplying a portion of the means to furnish it.
What are we to understand by sections of the country ?

My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier expressed the fear that under this Bill we might incur too large liabilities, but on the other hand my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) says that financial responsibilities involved in the construction of these docks are such that unless we give very liberal aid, such works will not be constructed at all. He says that, even with the aid we are now giving, we will not find companies prepared to undertake the risk and the responsibility.
Mr, INGRAM. I understood the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to say that this is a very old policy. Was it in existence before 1899 ?
I said that the original statute was passed twenty years ago, which my hon. friend may not consider very old.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The first Act was passed in 1882.

Has the hon. minister received any applications from any parties in Owen Sound with regard to increasing the capacity of the dry dock there ? And is it the intention of the government to give such parties any assistance ?

My hon. colleague the Minister of Public Works is the one to whom any such application would be addressed, and I would leave him to answer my hon. friend. As to whether any assistance would be given, I cannot say at present. It is not likely that these docks will be constructed close together. The cost of construction will be large, and if the demands of business are met in any one place, business men will not build another dock close by. Each case will be decided on its merits by the Governor General in Council, and the limitations I have suggested will regulate and restrict applications.

The reason why I asked whether any application had been made is because one of the strongest arguments used in favour of the Liberal candidate, that if elected, the government would furnish assistance for the purpose of enlarging the dry dock at Owen Sound. I would ask whether the government authorized the holding out of any such inducement on that occasion, and whether it is, the intention by this proposed Act to enlarge the dry docks at Owen Sound ?

If any application were made, it must have gone to the Minister of Public Works. If any application should come from Owen Sound or any part of Canada, it will be considered and dealt with on its merits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Owen Sound is a very much larger and more important business centre than Collingwood. The business done there is very large, and It is important that the dry dock should, be enlarged. This Bill is in the right direction. We require a larger dry dock in Owen Sound, and although the people there did not support me in the last election, to the extent they would, on account of these promises, I hope they will get the increased percentage on the same terms as Collingwood and other places mentioned by the Finance Minister.
It is now in order for the Minister of Customs to support the claims of Owen Sound, because when be was politically wrecked in South Brant he was put in dry docks in North Grey.

My hon. friend from North Grey was referred to the hon. Minister of Public Works for a reply to the question he put, as to whether any communication had been received from any party in Owen Sound respecting the giving of government aid for the enlargement of the dock there.

I will take a note of the question and inquire whether any such communications have been received at the department or not I cannot speak from memory. I did not make any promise and am not able to say what the policy of the government may be regarding this matter.

I did not understand the hon. minister to give a direct reply to the hon. member from Simcoe as to when this legislation by Order in Council on this particular subject was inaugurated. I see by the Bill that it repeals the clause of 1899. Was that the first legislation of this kind ?
T'he MINISTER OF CUSTOMS. No, that of 1882.
Was it on the same lines-that they could build a dock at any point they saw fit ?

Yes, the wording of the Act is precisely the same in that respect as the Act of 1882; and, although, by the amending Act, power was given to the government to give this subvention to a dock anywhere, as a matter of fact only one dock was subsidized under the Act.

I would like to ask what success this company has had in obtaining subscriptions to stock. I have a circular issued by that concern in August, 1902, which says :
The Dominion government recognizes the necessity in the public interest of an enlarged dry dock and has decided to grant a liberal subsidy for a term of twenty years ; the annual payments to be based upon the outlays made

upon the work, and to begin, upon its completion to the satisfaction of the government engineer. The Dominion government already grants a small bounty on the tonnage of steel steamships constructed in Canada.
This is a circular in which they ask subscriptions to the stock of the company.
I did not understand what document the hon. gentleman (Mr. Richardson) was reading from.
A document issued by the Collingwood Ship Building Company.

I have already stated that there is a dock in course of construction at Collingwood, that, no doubt, it would get the benefit of this Act. Hitherto they have had the benefit of the Act authorizing a payment of 2 per cent. If this Bill passes, no doubt the Collingwood Company will expect that their company will get the benefit of it, as the dock is nearing completion.

I understand that this Bill is specially designed for the benefit of the dry dock in the town of Collingwood. Now, there has been a dry dock in Owen Sound for twenty years, and I would like to know if this Bill applies equally to Owen Sound ? We want our dry dock enlarged. And, if this 3 per cent is to apply to the enlargement of other dry docks, we want it to be applied to the one in Owen Sound. As I said before, Owen Sound is the most important shipping point on Georgian 'bay, or, for that matter on the upper lakes. Hence, I would like a definite answer from the Minister of Finance.
I should like to be as definite as I can. I had the pleasure of visiting Owen Sound. It is a very charming place.
The hon. minister was warmly received there.

In many respects Owen Sound does its duty. My only regret is that some other parts of the county are not so sensible. ,1 would like to say to my hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Thomson) that the only difference that I know between the two cases is, that I am not aware that the owners of the dock at Owen Sound have made any application for aid, whereas the owners of the dock at Collingwood have done so. When people want aid of this kind, though they may go to the Minister of Public Works, they generally find time to call on the Minister of Finance and ask that he do not stand in their way. I have heard from the Collingwood and St. John people. It may be that there is an application from Owen Sound, although they neglected to call on me; but to the best of my knowledge, no application has been received from them. If an application comes, it will have to be dealt with on its merits.
93}

I may say that, even if the parties in control of the dry dock in North Grey failed to call on the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Finance did not forget to call on the electors of North Grey. We had the pleasure of a visit not only from the Finance Minister but also from the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) and the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick), and they received their answer. Nevertheless, we want to have a large dock in Owen Sound, and1 we want this Bill to apply to that work.

When I asked the Minister of Finance if this would apply to the Collingwood dock, I understood him to say that the Collingwood dock people did not know anything about it. Now, it appears that these people called on the hon. gentleman.
I did not say otherwise.
I may have misunderstood the hon. gentleman, but I certainly thought he said that they knew nothing about this legislation.

Sitting here at a little distance from the Minister of Finance, I am not sure that I have exactly heard his answers to hon. gentlemen opposite, and I want to understand clearly. I understand that this is simply a provision under which dry docks throughout the Dominion, if not too close together, may, on certain conditions, obtain government assistance. Is that .the point ?
That is the point, except that the Act does not say anything about their being too close together. That is left to the government, but there is no limit in the Bill.
It does not apply to Collingwood specially or to any other place specially ?
No.

The day before yesterday, I received a letter from large contractors in Vancouver, which city I have the honour to represent, saying that, since the government have decided to raise this subsidy from 2 to 3 per cent, they expect to build a large dock. There has never been any question about this matter with us. We know that when the government . bring down a Bill like this, they mean business. I think this is a very commendable proposition indeed, and I know that the fact of making this Bill law will result in our having a very large dock erected in Vancouver.

I would like to ask on what authority the directors of this Collingwood Company make this announcement, in their circular of 1902, that:

The government has decided to grant a liberal subsidy for a term of twenty years ; the annual payments to be based upon the outlays made upon the work, and to begin, upon its completion to the satisfaction of the government engineer.
In the same circular, later oil they say :
While we believe the improvements to be afforded by the additional capital will very materially increase the earnings of the company, we do not expect a higher dividend than six per cent per annum at present.
It would appear that they expect a large annual subsidy from the government for twenty years. Upon what authority did they make that announcement ?
The MINISTER OP, FINANCE. So far as concerns any past transaction the authority given to the government by legislation was to pay a subsidy of 2 per cent. From this time forward, if this Bill passes, we shall have authority to pay 3 per cent. The Collingwood dock is in course of construction, and it certainly is one of the docks that will have the aid of the government- there is no question about that. I think the information was given last year that the Collingwood dock was seeking and would receive aid. At all events it has been announced that the government would aid the Collingwood [DOT] dock.

I presume that the document quoted by the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Richardson) is the prospectus of the Collingwood Ship-building Company. Every toon, memtoer knows ttoat a dry dock company makes little or nottoing. A Ship-building company, on the other hand, may make the dividends referred to in the prospectus. I cannot speak as to this company, having nothing to do with it, good, bad or indifferent. But the hon. gentleman will see that the prospectus is in respeet to the building of ships, and one of the advantages which the company would have would be that they would be in a position to use this dry dock. The dry dock is only used to take a ship into for the purpose of repair. So, what the hon. gentleman has read applies to the prospective dividends in respect to the building of ships and not for the use of the dry clocks for other purposes than repairing ships.

I wish first to be understood as not speaking in any spirit of hostility to any grant being given to the dry dock at Collingwood. Although I live in a lake town which does a very much larger shipping business, so far at all events as grain goes, than the town of Collingwood, I admire the pluck and energy of the people of Collingwood in constructing the large dock there, and in establishing certain lines of passenger boats which run to that point and have their headquarters there, and which are certainly a credit, not only to Collingwood, but to the Dominion of Canada. Now, speaking of this prospectus which is before the House, it is headed ' The Collingwood Ship-building Company,' and it throws a little light on what the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy) has said, that this prospectus is not referrable solely to any money that is to be expended in the advancement or enlargement of the dock at that point.
Mr. McCarthy. I did not say it was not referrable to any money to be expended.

Not exclusively, he said; that is what I intended to convey. According to this document, the authorized capital is to be $2,000,000, which is referrable to the ship-building industry, and also to the establishment of a dry dock at that point. Of the capital issue there is paid up $550,000, and it is intended to issue $300,000 of new stock, of which $80,000 has already been subscribed. The date of that prospectus is August 12, 1902. Now, I assume that the largest part of this capital of $850,000 is to be put in the dry dock, and I have understood that the cost will nearly approach that sum. I understand that the company were of necessity compelled to purchase valuable real estate, so a part of the $850,000 would of necessity be expended for that purpose too. Now, the House must see that the amount to be expended upon the Collingwood dock as a whole will probably reach over half a million dollars. It was announced over a year ago that the Collingwood Dry Dock Company was to have the grant on these terms, then it may be taken for granted that any dock that is to he assisted, if this is to be taken as a precedent, must of necessity cost half a million dollars. Now, I submit that when a Bill is brought down following this resolution, it should be firmly laid down in the Bill that the cost of the dock must be a certain amount, otherwise what will be the effect ? Let me tell the Minister of Finance that in the province of Ontario the people have gone mad on what is known as the bonusing system, rival towns seeking to promote their interests will give bonuses to manufacturing concerns. We have there within a distance of seventy-five miles, on the coast line, the towns of Owen Sound, Collingwood and Midland, all ambitious. And if the government are going to grant such liberal subsidies as under this Bill they will grant, of necessity the result will be a great competition between these towns. I submit it is fair to the people of the town of Midland to have the government announce a line of policy, so that we may set our house in order and get ready for the government grant. When the Bill is brought down, it should state distinctly what amount must he the cost of the dock before it will be assisted by the government, otherwise it would he giving the government in advance a great deal of political leverage, because a certain town may be preferred by the government, and therefore get the benefit, while others may he cast to one side. I submit that when the
Bill Is brought down, there should be in it a clear cut statement as to what amount must be expended on the dock before it will receive assistance under this Act.

There is another remark to be made in connection with this legislation. The Finance Minister is right in saying that the principle of making grants to dry docks by Order in Council was established in 1882, but the grant was then limited to $10,000. In 1899, after hon. gentlemen opposite came into power, they made it $20,000 ; but the necessities of Collingwood have become such that they now treble the grant and make it $30,000. Now, I can conceive that there may be eases, and probably this is one, where a small amount might be granted by Order in Council, say $10,000. The hon. gentleman also states what is no doubt correct, that when only $10,000 was granted, only one dry dock claimed assistance. But I object entirely to legislation of this kind, especially when you go beyond small amounts. Here the Finance Minister is asking us to authorize the government to issue as many million dollars as they please, provided some one will undertake to construct a dry dock. Now, when it conies to an amount that is equal to a capitalization of a million dollars, I think parliament ought to be consulted. When $10,000 was the limit the Conservative government found it was quite sufficient. Why cannot this government get up a scheme and bring it before parliament, providing that every sum to be granted must be subject to the sanction of parliament ? This system is wrong in principle, it is liable to be abused, and it makes people suspicious of such a power in the hands of the government when they can exercise it by Order in Council. There is no better illustration of the objectionable character of this system than is furnished by the town of Collingwood. Does my hon. friend who represents it, and represents it well, claim that it is his ability alone that has made that town a Liberal instead of a Conservative town ? There has been a lot of money spent and a lot of promises made in regard to public works in Owen Sound and vicinity about election times, not the last election, but the previous one, where we heard statements about * cold justice ' and 'warm justice,' and so on. We have a right to suspect that this power which is now sought may be exercised. I won't say it will be, but it puts the government of the day, I do not care which party may be in power, in the position of being suspected of using that power for political advantage. Any legislation of that kind, which enables a government by Order in Council to control public funds for party purposes, I am opposed to, especially if the amount is at all large. I approve of. the restrictions such as my hon. friend from Simcoe mentions : I approve of assistance being limited to deserving places ; but I think that before |
sums exceeding $10,000 are granted, parliament should be consulted before granting the money. In that case nobody could suspect the government, nobody would have a right to impute improper motives, and the government would be following a sound constitutional principle. There is no reason why it would not be just as easy to form a company to build a dry dock when the grant of a subsidy is subject to parliament as it would be if the government granted the subsidy by Order in Council. Again I say, I object to the principle of giving this power to the government without surrounding it with constitutional safeguards, more particularly when the subsidy amounts to a considerable sum.
I beg to say a word on behalf of the Collingwood people. I am largely responsible for the work that has been carried on there.
I am not saying a word against the Collingwood people.

When I undertook to recommend to my colleagues the construction of the works at Collingwood, the late Mr. Dalton McCarthy was a member of parliament. He was not then a strong supporter of the government. He was quite an independent member of this House. I was invited to a banquet at the board of trade. Banquets have something good about them, and that Collingwood banquet was a great one indeed. I found around the table energetic, sterling business men. They represented to me that if some encouragement were given to them they would do their share to promote the development of the port, one of the most important ports on the great lakes. I came down to Ottawa fully convinced that this was a deserving! case. I represented to my colleagues that it was important that the government should carry out the improvements that had been undertaken there years and years ago and which were not completed. My colleagues were good enough to agree with the recommendations I made then. The improvements have been carried out. What has been the result of these improvements ? The population of the town of Collingwood has nearly doubled and large industries have sprung up. The people of Collingwood have done their part and for the improvements we have made there we have been paid in hard cash in the shape of development and progress. Let my hon. friend permit me to tell him that there was no political cajoling about Collingwood. These Collingwood men are business men before everything else. The government treated them fairly and they have acted in good faith. These were energetic men. They gave their votes to my hon. friend here (Mr. McCarthy). It may be my fault to a certain extent. I do not regret it. There are thousands and thou-| sands of people in this country who have

no strong party leanings and who are business men before everything else. Well, in Collingwood I feel that we have dealt with men of that character. These men were Conservatives in the past.
They were harbourites.

What I think is that they will always vote right. I am glad to say that they proceeded energetically with their part of the work. They had promised me that if the government would help them they would erect large works. They are to day building ships on a large scale. My hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) has settled there. He has erected a large mill and there are other large industries established at Collingwood. The population of the town has doubled.
I do not object to the expenditure. I said that this was a desirable expenditure but that there was such a large amount involved that it should first be approved by parliament.

As to the Order in Council I am no longer on the treasury benches and it is not for me to defend that part of the argument, but after having been six and a half years a minister I believe I can properly say in the light of experience that I have the conviction that governments can as a rule be trusted.
Cannot ?

Yes, governments as a rule can be trusted-I say it again -whatever party they belong to. I do not believe that there enough men at the Council Board to do wrong. That is my experience. I have no interest in stating that. I have no political interest to serve in stating that as a public man for the edification of the people and also for their education, perhaps. Let me say again, and I will be borne out by those who have been Ministers of the Crown, that while there may be unworthy ministers, when you have to deal with the whole government there is not much to be feared.

I find that on the 22nd January a banquet was tendered at Collingwood by the board of trade and that on that occasion the hon. Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) was present as their guest. It was only fitting and proper that any needs of the town should be brought before the minister and I see that Mr. John Long who occupied the chair on that occasion made. the complaint that he thought the town was suffering. His complaint was this :
Now, as they were aware, the dock was being still further enlarged, and when finished would be equipped so as to accommodate the largest vessels floating on the lakes. He hoped the government would see its way to pay a greater per cent of its cost than two per cent which bad been promised. He wished the government Hon. Mr. TARTE.
would take over the dock and pay for its cost, and the town would operate it.
Mr. Long then went on to speak about the ship building industry in that town, and as to the future of the industry he expressed very grave doubts and misgivings. He pointed out that they were brought into competition with the British ships and he said :
At the same time British built vessels were allowed to come here and navigate in competition without any tax being imposed on them.
Mr. Long laid down two complaints; first there was the question of assistance to the dry dock and then the question of competition between the British vessels which were being brought upon the great lakes and those which were built at Collingwood. When the hon. Postmaster General came to reply he endeavoured to soothe the feelings of the Collingwood people present on that occasion. The hon. Postmaster General gave them an assurance as to what was to be done in respect to one of their complaints, but it will turn out, as I will show, that the hon. gentleman was entirely wrong in his view as to what could be done for the people of Collingwood. What did the hon. gentleman tell them ? He seems to have skimmed very lightly over the question of the dock, but he took up the question of duties on ships and he then and there told the people of Collingwood in his own language that they were to be given substantial assistance, that they were to be protected in the matter of the ship-building industry. Here is what the hon. gentleman said :
As to the question of duties on ships, raised by Mr. Long, it seemed to him that no political economist could justify admitting free a finished article and taxing the raw material.
What did that mean ? It meant that the hon. Postmaster General was holding out to these people hope that British ships would have certain restrictions placed upon them or that certain concessions would be made under the tariff in favour of the Collingwood sihip-building industry. What position are the government in to-day ? It is a question whether the hon. Postmaster General by his words meant that the government would be in a position to prohibit by this restriction of which he spoke, the entrance of British ships upon the great lakes, and yet he certainly must have meant that or he meant that the raw materials which were used in the construction of ships would have their duties reduced. The hon. Postmaster General evidently came down to his colleagues. By them he was told that it was impossible to place a restriction on British vessels coming upon the great lakes and as the government were afraid apparently to reduce the duties on the raw materials entering into the construction of ships they are endeavouring to carry out some of the promises of the hon. Postmaster General and now we find that one

of these promises is being carried out by increasing this bonus from two per cent to three per cent.

There is not the slightest connection between the resolution now before the House and my references at the Collingwood banquet in question, to the condition described by speakers as to the manufacture and importation of ships-not the slightest understanding^ between the government and the Collingwood people. Both these questions stand entirely on their own merits separately and apart, and they are to be dealt with by the government separately and apart.
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, without wandering any farther from the question, permit me to call your attention to the fact that this is a dock Bill, and while no doubt there are questions of duties on ships and ship-building aids, which are all very important, I should like to confine this discussion if I can to the matter before the committee.

It is very gratifying to find that hon. members on both sides of the House appreciate what is being done in the way of development in the town of Collingwood. The ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) tells us, that after his first interview with the citizens of Collingwood he was impressed that they were an energetic business people, and that if they were encouraged they would develop the resources of that town and district in a manner which would be a credit to themselves and to all Canada. He tells us that having come to that conclusion he did aid the citizens of Collingwood. Truly, he did. And as a result of that aid Collingwood has embarked in a very large enterprise, namely the Collingwood Ship-building Company, which at the present time is employing seven hundred men where some years ago not a man was employed. They have that line of steamers) to which my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has referred, and these steamers carry thousands of passengers to the town each year. That line can only be successfully operated by keeping our harbour in a proper condition. In view of what the Finance Minister has said, I do not intend to wander further from the subject, than to say, that when the Postmaster General was in Collingwood .it was an accepted fact that the Collingwood Shipbuilding Company wa s to be assisted in the building of a dry dock, and at that time this increased aid was spoken of. Therefore when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) said that the Postmaster General was skating over very thin ice at that time, he is not correct. The only question before the people then was a question of giving increased aid to the dry dock, and that is being accomplished to-day by the legislation
now before the House. But, Sir* that increased aid is not only for the town of Collingwood, it is to extend throughout the whole Dominion in favour of any worthy proposition for the building of a dry dock. Let me say that there is no money in the establishment of a dry dock per se. The ship-building company can only use the dry dock for the purpose of repairing ships, and the money which can be made out of shipbuilding-if money can be made out of the industry at all-is in the actual building of new ships. Is it not an argument in favour of this very small increase, that this shipbuilding company at the very inception of its business is able to find employment for seven hundred men; is it not an argument that that employment will be extended and work and wages provided for the people of Collingwood who by their labour will assist in the carrying on of this enterprise ? The Collingwood company has already built three ships, and a great many ships now plying upon the upper lakes which hitherto had to go to the United States come there now to be repaired. We will therefore divert from the United States the repairing of these ships, and we will to that extent benefit our own country. That, Sir, is a laudable enterprise; it is an enterprise which will receive encouragement from the Canadian people when it is fully understood. I am gratified, Sir, that so far as Collingwood is concerned, we never can be looked upon with that suspicion which was suggested by the hon. member for Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale). This question has been very fully discussed, and I think we can take it for granted that very little objection will be offered by any member in this House to giving the Collingwood Ship-building Company the aid which has been asked by them.

I think, Sir, that the country is beginning to view with alarm the policy of increasing subsidies to companies of this character. I have in my hand a circular issued by this Collingwood Company last August, in which they speak of being able to pay dividends of 0 per cent per annum, and the circular states that the policy of the directors will be to still further increase their works and earn greater dividends. They say they have no hesitation in recommending the stock as a sound business investment which is likely to become more valuable within a reasonable time. I believe, Sir, that the people of the country at large without respect to politics, have no objection to reasonable encouragement- being given to large business enterprises for the development of our industries and commerce. But there is a feeling of unrest and a feeling of alarm, when companies of large capital like this apply to the government to receive assistance which will enable them to pay larger dividends than that already paid by the Collingwood Ship-building Company. It is no wonder that when they are seeking such

help from the government, they can give banquets to the ministers when they go to visit Collingwood.
It was not the company that gave the entertainment. It was the board of trade and the municipal council of Collingwood which organized the banquet.	'

I suppose the company was not at all interested in it, and took no part in it. I find it father difficult to believe that. I know that the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCarthy) has made an attempt to separate the Ship-building Company of Collingwood from the dry dock company.
I did no such a thing.

As far as I can learn they are one and the same company, and the earnings of the one are the earnings of the other.
Mr. McCarthy. Decidedly.
I think, Sir, the members of this House will feel it incumbent upon them to pause before they increase the subsidies which have already been granted in this direction.

I cannot allow the insinuation to pass, that the ship-building company was responsible for the entertainments which have been given in the town of Collingwood. That statement is absolutely without foundation. These banquets have been given by the citizens of Collingwood represented by the municipal council and the board of trade, and every man who went to that banquet paid for his ticket. It is that instinct of enterprise which has made the people of Collingwood what they are to-day. They do not sit down and wait for a company to entertain ministers or others when they visit the town. The citizens do that themselves and they pay for it themselves. I refrained from replying to the statement of the hon. member for Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale), but in view of the insinuations he has thrown out, perhaps the question of politics can be referred to. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) has said that as a result of the treatment which Collingwood has received at the hands of the government, Collingwood sent a member to support the Reformers in this parliament. It is true that I have supported the government on most questions, but I supported the government because I thought the government was right. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) knows very well that the town of Collingwood has been voting for the name which I bear since 1878. and I do not expect that the insinuations which are sometimes hurled across the floor of this House, will ever get the people of Collingwood to change their allegiance.

In respect to how many places have applications been Mr. RICHARDSON.
made to the government for an increase of this subsidy ? How many docks are likely to be built under the provisions of this proposed,' Bill, as far as the government is at present aware ?

I have already mentioned that the only places from which we have had applications are Col-liugwood, Ontario and St. John, N.B. In the case of Collingwood, the matter was discussed in times past and it was agreed that we should aid that dock to the extent of the legislation then on the statute-book which was 2 per cent. In the case of St. John, N.B., no progress has been made, but they are endeavouring to establish a company and we have reason to believe that with this increased aid a company will be established to construct a dock in St. John. Reference was made before my bom friend (Mr. Borden) entered the House, to the position of Montreal under this Bill, and 1'mentioned that if the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal should desire to avail themselves of this method of construction they would be a body corporate and would be entitled to come under the operation of this Act. There may be other places in which docks are thought of, but I think I am correct in saying that these two are the only cases that have been brought before the government. If there are any others, of course we will be prepared to look into tfiem on their merits, upon application being made.

I understand that there is a dry dock in existence iu Collingwood for a number of years which at present they are rebuilding and extending. 1 do not see how this resolution can cover that case. Here is a dock partially built and you propose to give aid to it presumedly on the approval of plans at the present time.
Although there was a dock of a certain character at Collingwood for years, this is practically a new dock.
Absolutely a new dock.

It may be treated as a new dock. If we had subsidized the Collingwood dock originally, then we would be obliged to treat this as an extension, but the original dock at Collingwood was a small concern and never received government aid. It comes under the operation of the existing law as a new dock, and not as an extension of the old one.

That makes the case >
a great deal worse. Here is a dock which is already in existence.
Mr. McCarthy. It is not.

A part of it is in
existence.
There is a hole there.

A part of it is in existence and some of the works are in

existence at the present time. The hon. gentleman intends to advance money for the purpose of purchasing the whole of it, or the value already existing is taken into consideration. It is not like a new structure.
Yes, it is a new dock altogether.
The Finance Minister says there is an old dock at present being repaired, and he looks on it in the light of a reconstruction.
The old dock has practically disappeared, and the aid under this Act will be upon the expenditure not on the old structure, but on the new.
Is there any part of the old one being rebuilt ?
A very trifling part.
There is no building going on, is there ?

Yes, it is rapidly approaching completion. It is practically a new work. The hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Richardson) argued as if this was a bonus to a company engaged in a private enterprise. The Oollingwood dock, and all other docks which will receive aid under this Act are public docks, rendering a public service. No one who is acquainted with the importance of our inland navigation will fail to recognize the urgent need of providing dry dock accommodation on the upper lakes. The hon. member for South Grey does not find a supporter of his views in his colleague from East Grey (Mi-. Sproule) whose criticism was, not that this was an unwise measure, but that we were not proposing sufficient aid. The hon. member for South Grey says the aid is too liberal ; the hon. member for East Grey says it should be more liberal. It is difficult for us to reconcile the views of these hon. gentlemen. This money will not only aid the ship-building industry, but it will be useful to all who navigate the upper lakes; and under the proposed amendment to the law- it is not before the committee at the present time, but will come in due course-the government will have full control over the rates to be charged for the use of the dry dock. This in itself will ensure fair rates, and prevent any extortion, or any private tapi-tal that may be invested in the work being unduly remunerative to the investors. When an estimate comes to be made of what rates should be permitted to be charged, a proper account will be taken of the amount of private capital invested in the enterprise, and the amount of the probable earnings, and the rates will be so fixed as only to admit of the proper maintenance of the work and a reasonable dividend to those who contribute capital to the enterprise.
What is the length of the proposed new dock ?

It is about 500 feet. I was at Collingwood in the month of January ; ' my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) was present at the same time ; and I am sure that he was as gratified as I was at the great industrial activity we saw in Collingwood. It gave me the greatest possible pleasure to see the prosperity of that town through the enterprise of its citizens. They were building two magnificent ships, capable of carrying 250,000 bushels of wheat at least. Those ships were expected to be launched in the course of a few months, and I believe one of them is now about to be launched ; and the people are reaching out for further contracts. The construction of such a dock as this will not only aid those who wish to use it, but will also make possible an extension of the ship-building industry at Collingwood, a branch of industry of the greatest importance. There are iron and steel works in operation on the north shore, in the Sault Ste. Marie district, and in many ways the general public will be advantaged by the construction of this dock.

What was the length of the old dock ?
Sir. SlcCARTHY. 100 or 150 feet.

It is because of the knowledge I have of the difficulties which the shipping industry on the Georgian Bay and the upper lakes have had to contend with that I approve of this measure. For many years attempts were made to induce the government to aid in the construction of a dry dock at Collingwood or Owen Sound, but they would not grant sufficient aid. The assistance they proposed was so small that capitalists would not undertake the work, although the shipping on the Georgian bay and the upper lakes was rapidly increasing. Vessels needing the use of a dry dock had to go to the American side. The dock at Collingwood would not accommodate one of the Canadian Pacific Railway boats, which are over 300 feet long, while the dock is less than 100 feet.
The dock at Collingwood, before the change took place, would accommodate one of the Canadian Pacific boats.

The vessel in the dock was partly in and partly out ; the dock could not properly accommodate it. Therefore, there was need to devise a means whereby a dry dock could be provided on the Georgian bay. If Owen Sound avails itself of this government aid, all the better, though it may be inadvisable to have two docks in the same district. If Collingwood raises the capital for a dry dock, so much to its credit. The principle

of tlie measure is a good one, and if it lias any defect it is that it does not go far enough, the amount being too small. We gave a large subsidy for a dry dock at Kingston, and for the graving dock at Es-quimalt.
They were built by the government.

Yes, they were practically built by the government; but on the upper lakes and the Georgian bay, where the shipping interest is greater than it is in any other part of Canada, the government have given no assistance at all. When they propose to give it, I can only say that for my part, I endorse the proposition, and the only complaint I have is that they do not give greater assistance.

The hon. gentleman who has just sat down does not answer the point I raised at all ; and my knowledge of his contrary nature is the only reason I venture to say a word in reply. My point has not reference to the amount or the place at all. I said that I knew of no more desirable object to which to devote public money, and I think Collingwood is entitled to a share of it in the nature of things. But I object to the principle of this Bill. I object to establishing a precedent for allowing any government by Order in Council to cover this whole country with dry docks, without submitting their proposals to parliament. I did not object to the sum of $10,000 proposed by the Conservative government ; but this was a small amount. Hon. gentlemen opposite propose to grant three times as much. Judging by the past, I do not know that $30,000 will be enough for Collingwood ; but what I say is that the government should bring down a grant, as they did in the case of Kingston and Esquimalt, and let parliament vote it. This grant of $30,000 a year, capitalized is equal to $1,000,000.
It is only twenty years, and twenty times $30,000 make $600,000 payable every twenty years.
With accumulated interest ?
No.

Only $600,000. Why, I have seen this House detained for weeks, when we were in power, over an item of $5,000. What I wish to protest against is this principle of expenditure by Order in Council. There is a feeling abroad that the government are going into lavish expenditure simply because they have a full treasury. In my opinion, fhat is the time to help the people by cutting off the duties on materials that do not need protection. I am not raising my voice against the expenditure itself in this particular instance, but what I am opposed to is giving Mr. SPROtTLE.
authority to the government to dispose of large sums outside the control of parliament. It is contrary to the principles of responsible government and it lays the government open to suspicion. Our people do not want tlie government to be put in a position, that, even when they do right, they are liable to be suspected. Take this Collingwood item, if we were asked to vote $30,000 per year over a period of twenty years, for a dry dock there, I would be the last to object, but what I do object to is the passing of a resolution of this kind, which will put it in the power of the government to expend, without the direct sanction of parliament, such an amount for the construction of dry docks whenever they may see tit. I may be old-fashioned in my ideas, I may be too much wedded to the fine old principles of constitutional British government and legislation. But these principles have done good service for a thousand years, and I do not want to see any one of them swept away, and would rather be thought old-fashioned than allow legislation, such as is now proposed, to pass without protest.

My hon. friend takes exception to the principle involved in this measure, and no doubt he is now sincere. But I would like to know when he experienced this change of heart ? He objects to the principle of allowing the Governor General in Council to decide when the aid provided by this resolution should be granted, but when did he first discover that this was not sound policy ?
When the amount became large.
We are not changing the principle of the law. That law was passed with the approval of my hon. friend. All we are doing is changing the percentage from two to three.
I was not in the House in 1882.
My hon. friend was in the government when this law was on the statutes, and during fourteen years he saw nothing in it to criticise.
The limit was then

It is the principle that my hon. friend, is discussing and not the amount. It was the government which he supported that adopted the principle, and incorporated it in our statutes. My hon. friend entered that government, knowing that that statute was in existence, knowing what was in it, and he allowed it to remain without any objection on his part. The principle of that legislation was a good one until to-day, when suddenly it becomes most objectionable. When was it that this hon. gentleman became con-

verted into such an ardent defender and advocate of popular rights ? Is it only since he has been in opposition and unable therefore to give effect to his views ? But the proper time for him to have given some practical effect to his ideas was when he had the power to do so. What is the use of a man holding such strong views and refraining from giving any expression to them until he knows that his protests can have no effect ?
The hon. gentleman might ask himself the same question. When did he become converted ?
I am now dealing with my hon. friend from South Norfolk, and while I am not questioning his sincerity to-day, I should like to know when his convictions became so radically and suddenly changed ?

My hon. friend finds fault with my hon. friend from South Norfolk for his change of principle. I think that the hon. minister might apply (his own remarks to himself. He was the most rabid of opponents of all these Acts of parliament and resolutions, passed in this House in 1882, and at other times, giving the government the power to spend money by Order in Council. But this principle, which he formerly held, he has dropped, as he has done every other, since he came into office. We are now dealing with the question of giving $10,000 per year for the building of a dry (lock, or two per cent on the cost of its construction now. What is now proposed is $30,000 per year or 3 per cent on the cost.
The principle is not changed.

The granting of a small sum may be harmless in itself, but when you increase that sum and make it a large amount, then the question of principle becomes a very serious one. What may be indifferent when a small expenditure is at stake may become a very serious matter when it involves a large expenditure. I have in my hand a prospectus of the company in question, which states :
The company possesses at. Collingwood the only dry dock on the upper lakes, in Canada, capable ot accommodating large vessels. It is proposed to increase its capacity so as to enable it to take the largest vessels trading, or likely to trade, on these waters.
They only intend to increase the capacity of the dry dock.
What is the date of that prospectus ?

August 12, 1902. The company go further and say that they have made an arrangement with the Dominion government for the purpose of assisting them in this work.
The Dominion government recognizes the necessity in the public interest, of an enlarged dry dock, and have decided to grant a liberal subsidy for a term of twenty years ; the annual payments to be based upon the outlays made upon the work.
The payments are therefore to be made upon the work of enlargement and not upon the whole work. But the hon. Minister of Finance and the hon. Postmaster General led us to believe that this is an entirely new work.
Practically, it is.
They state in this prospectus, in which they ask people to subscribe money, that they have a dry dock already, and that all they need to expend in this respect is enough to enlarge that dry dock.
Will the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) allow me to make an explanation with regard to that ?
Certainly.

I know nothing about that prospectus. But I can quite recall a statement made to me by people in Collingwood when I was there in January last. I think the statement was made by Mr. John Long, though I am not very sure. At all events, one of the gentlemen who knew all about this plan took me down to where the work was going on. He showed me the new work and told me that at first they had expected to be able to utilize part of the old work, but when they endeavoured to do so, they found i't impossible, and they had to do away with the old structure-
At what time was the hon. minister there ?

In January last. And the hon. gentleman lias read from a prospectus issued, I think, in August, last. Evidently, at that time, they expected to be able to use part of the old wharf, but afterwards found that this could not be done.

I know nothing about the circumstances, and did not even know that there was a dry dock there. But I know that this is the prospectus on which they raised money in the market, and I understand that at present their shares are listed in the stock exchange in Toronto. But, the statement made in this prospectus is that they had made an arrangement with the government for an advance
That is under the old law.

The prospectus states that the Dominion government recognizes the necessity in the public interest

of au enlarged dry dock and lias decided to grant a liberal subsidy for a term of twenty years. And the bon. minister finds fault with the hon. member from South Norfolk for saying that this amounts to a million dollars.
I did not find fault with that.

The hon. gentleman said there was only $600,000. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) is absolutely correct-a guarantee of $30,000 a year for twenty years, when you have the undertaking also, is worth in any market in the world one million dollars.
How could that be ?

This $30,000 a year for twenty years guarantees the interest for that length of time which enables them to borrow to the full value of this $30,000 a year. Then they have the undertaking, which is an additional security.
They could sell it readily for a million dollars.
Certainly. Is that not correct ?
No.
I would like to know how the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir William Mulock) makes that out.

An annuity of $30,000 for twenty years may have various advantages to the person who is to enjoy it. But we are dealing with it from the standpoint of the Canadian taxpayer, who is to pay it. An annuity of $30,000 a year for twenty years amounts, on its face, to $000,000. But, this is to be reduced to its present cash value. An actuary would estimate that for you-the present cash value of $600,000 payable in twenty annual instalments and calculated at three per cent would be so much less, how much less I do not know. The taxpayer of Canada is not paying $000,000, but only the present value of that sum paid under the provisions named. But I will add to my hon. friend's argument for him. We are considering now only one dock, but, under this Bill there may be other docks. My hon. friend has the opportunity of magnifying this fund by multiplying it by as many docks as his imagination leads him to believe will be brought into existence. He could work up a large bill in that way.

The hon. gentleman is right looking at it from the point of view he speaks of-the present cash value of the sum to be paid by the government. But we are looking at it from the point of view of the advantage to the men who receive the money. It was from that Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
point of view that my hon. friend from South Norfolk was looking at it, and from that point of view he is quite correct. But let me refer to the point to which I drew the attention of the Minister of Finance, and which he tried to get over by saying that this was virtually a reconstructed work. But, first of all, before they are entitled to any money, before any arrangement can be made, the plan must be approved by the engineer of the department. I understand that the work is nearly completed, or, at least is well under way. How, then, can this apply to this particular case? The work is to be built under the supervision of the engineer attached to the Public Works Department or there must be a report of the engineer that this money has been expended on the work.
Would the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) allow me a moment ?
Certainly.
Before that dock at Collingwood was put under construction, Mr. Coste, an officer of the department was authorized to supervise the work.
Is he on it ?
Certainly.
Was au agreement made ?
Certainly.
An Order in Council ?
An Order in Council passed when I was in office. The work is . perfectly regular.
We shall be delighted to get the whole information from the government.

Perhaps I may be allowed to suggest that the difficulty is that my hon friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) came in late, and so had not the benefit of the information that was given to the hon. gentlemen who were here. I stated that we had agreed to aid the Collingwood dock to the extent of two per cent.

But here is a new agreement. The old Act which limits the amount to two per cent on the amount spent, or in this case, $20,000. But there is a subsidiary agreement, evidently, by which the government promised to bring in legislation for the purpose of paying three per cent.
I did not say that.

Here is the resolution. Here is the expression of the intention of the government, and we have

the announcement from the government that it is intended to apply to this particular dry dock. They made a bargain but they were unable to carry it out under the old Act, and now they find it necessary to have further legislation-
They could not deliver the goods.
For some reason which I do not know
Banquet.

I have the assurance of the hon. member for Simcoe that none of the parties had anything to do with that, and I accept his statement. However, there must have been a bargain to give them assistance beyond that authorized by the old statute. It is time, in any case, that this system of grants by Order in Council, all this system of governing the country by Orders in Council was done away with. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) twits the hon. member for South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) with being a supporter of this system in 1882. We have discarded those principles. The country has advanced, as the hon. Minister of Finance has assured us. This is a growing and a better time in intelligence and otherwise, and it is time that this kind of legislation was wiped off the statute-book- this governing of the country by Orders in Council and granting large subsidies to corporations or individuals without the direct sanction and support of parliament.

The discussion has taken a rather wide range ; and it strikes me, Mr. Chairman, that the criticisms of hon. gentlemen opposite in relation to this matter are somewhat captious and unfair. I am pleased to find that my hon. friend from South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) has imbibed such correct and constitutional impressions with regard to the expenditure of money by Order in Council. It reminds me of the old days in opposition when a great deal of capital was made out of criticisms of that kind, and when perhaps we were not in possession of facts which might have modified our opinions with regard to the criticisms that were made. The government of which both my hon. friend from South Norfolk and my hon. friend from Lanark were supporters, distinctly recognized this principle in the matter of grants to dry docks. The principle of granting $10,000 to aid a dry dock in 1882 was on all fours with the principle of granting $30,000 in 1903, under the changed circumstances with regard to transportation, the size of vessels built and the extraordinary size of the dry docks necessary. I can see, Sir, no particular objection to the plan adopted under these resolutions on which a Bill is to be founded. I have confidence enough in the members of the ministry who meet in Council and discuss these questions
