in a business-like way, I have confidence enough in their ability to arrive at a correct opinion, to believe that in an adjustment of business matters of this kind they could be fairly trusted with the discharge of that duty. I have confidence enough in their honesty to believe that they .would not stoop to anything irregular or improper in granting subsidies of this character and under the provisions of this resolution. I am not able to see how, if they were disposed to do so, it would be convenient or possible for them to travel very far from the paths of rectitude.
The building of a dry dock is a business proposition. The aid granted under this resolution by the government is not sufficient to build it. It is merely the granting of a certain amount of aid which will enable the parties engaged in the operation of building a dock, perhaps to float their bonds to secure the resources necessaiy for the purpose of going on and constructing a dock that otherwise they would be unable to do. I do not think it is necessary to come to the House of Commons with every separate and distinct proposition for the construction of a dry dock in the Dominion of Canada. Here is a general principle laid down. The government is protected in the request made upon it to grant aid by the fact that the parties making that request have got to put up more money than the government does, they have got to show their good faith and confidence in the scheme hy investing the major part of the money necessary to construct the dry dock. An annuity of 3 per cent for twenty years capitalized, does not amount to the aggregate of that annuity for that time. Six hundred thousand dollars, the maximum sum of $30,000 per annum for twenty years, falls far short of the capitalized sum of $600,000.
Now, Sir, in the discussion of this question we have had exhibited here certain local jealousies, jealousies between different ports on the Georgian bay. There is Owen Sound, there is Collingwood, there is Midland, all thriving towns, all of them important shipping points, and it is necessary for the commercial wants of the Georgian bay to have a first-class dry dock in each one of these towns. One dock would serve the purpose as well as three ; but if one would hardly have business enough to make it a paying investment, not enough in the locality which has put itself in the position of building a dry dock, which would be sufficient to meet the commercial wants of that section of the great lakes, wthy, that locality has a just cause in appealing to the government for aid, and the government is warranted in giving to that place or locality the aid necessary for constructing that dry dock.
Now, what are the circumstances upon the Georgian bay ? There has recently been developed on that bay a large commerce, a large carrying trade in grain, a large passenger traffic, a large business in lumber,

and there will be a large business in iron ore, a large business in various departments. There has been erected at Collingwood one of the finest ship-building plants on the continent, that has already turned out two large vessels, as large as the largest class of carriers on the upper lakes, a plant that is turning out two vessels now, and is prepared to add from year to year to the mercantile marine of the Dominion three or four of these vessels. This is an enterprise that is a credit to Canada, an enterprise that ought to command our respect and appeal to our pride. Well, it has been found necessary to have in connection with this business, resources and accommodations for the docking of these vessels. It was not creditable to us that vessels of this class had to be sent to Detroit, or Cleveland, or Buffalo, for repairs. We had no dry dock upon the upper lakes that would accommodate vessels of this class. One is being built at Collingwood and is approaching completion, a dry dock ample for all the purposes that will be required in docking the large class of vessels that sail the upper lakes.
Now, the objection is raised by the hon. member for North Lanark that part of this dry dock is an old dry dock, and, for some reason I am not able to understand, he says because this company is making use of a hole that has been dug there for the old dry dock, they are not entitled to this subsidy. Even if the walls of the old dry dock were capable of being utilized for the new dock, I am unable to understand why it would not be to all intents and purposes a new dry dock. But they were not capable of being utilized-they had to be torn down ; all they could use of the old dry dock was a little amount of excavation, the cross walls of the old dry dock had to be built entirely new, and to all intents and purposes it is a new dry dock. All the advantage derived by the company from the existence of the old dock was infinitesimal. Under these circumstances, I think we are wasting our time here in haggling over this matter in the way we are doing. I do not think it would be a workable method even to allow these things to drift along, and, before the government will give any assurance of aid to a company that desired to build a dry dock or make improvements of this character, to wait until parliament could be consulted. If that had been the case'with this dry dock, it would not have been constructed even now, it would not be built perhaps for years hence, and it would have been a great loss to the public interest of the Georgian bay and a loss to the commercial interests of the Dominion for that delay to have occurred.
I was in Collingwood last week and saw this dry dock. It is a creditable work. The company had to buy land right in the heart of the town to extend their dock landward. They have got an enormous plant there. In connection with the ship-building they Mr. CHARLTON.
had to take up a railway track and move it landward, they had to destroy buildings to find room for their excavation, and they have gone on here and built a dry dock of a first-class character, a dry dock that will dock a man-of-war, that will dock a vessel with a carrying capacity of 300,000 bushels. The whole of the commercial interests of Georgian bay and the upper lakes realize that this is a work of the utmost importance, realize that it is a work that reflects great credit on the enterprise of the town of Collingwood. If Collingwood is enjoying the prosperity it deserves, it is because it has had wide-awake business men that grasped the situation with courage, men who are ready to invest their money, men whom the government might legitimately aid in promoting the construction of a work of this kind. The town has subscribed a large amount, the town has stood ready at all times to promote any of these enterprises that were calculated to increase its prosperity. The result has been the location of the Cramp steel works there.
They are pretty sick of it now.

They will be all right in regard to that. They may be sick of it but they will, I hope, have reason to be gratified that they have invested that money. I think if we look at this thing from the proper standpoint, if we realize that a dry dock is absolutely needed and needed now and that it could not have been had now if we had resorted to the method recommended by the hon. member for Sonth Simcoe (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) and the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) if we realized that the commercial interests of the Georgian bay require that improvement, that there is no investment of public money asked for in this session that will produce more satisfactory results or that will be more necessary in the public interests than that which is covered by these resolutions, if we realize all these things, then, we had better drop this discussion and be thankful that we have this ship-building plant and this magnificent dry dock accommodation at Collingwood which is sufficient for the upper lakes and the effect of which can only be to promote the commerce of this Dominion.

I am glad to observe that the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) seems to have a higher opinion of politics and politicians in this country than that which I am told he expressed a few weeks ago in a sermon which he delivered, I think, in this city.
That applied equally to both sides.

I understand the hon. gentleman, of course, being on that side of the House, was speaking out of his more especial knowledge concerning his own party and indulged only in a surmise

so far as this side of the House is concerned. But, I am glad to observe that the confidence of the hon. gentleman has been somewhat restored and that he agrees entirely with the very proper remarks of the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that there may be confidence extended even to a government such as this. I understand that the remarks of the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Hag-gart)- in regard to a dock partly constructed, or to a dock partly in existence, were intended in the sense that he desired to have this resolution drawn in such a way that it would be workable in regard to the Colling-wood dock which has more especially been mentioned in this discussion. Any observations I have in regard to it are intended in the same sense. This resolution could hardly apply to a dock which has already been constructed. I do not know whether X correctly understood the hon. member for North Norfolk when he said that this dock was partly constructed now.
Yes, it is far advanced.

Of course, I have not considered the question very carefully, but it would seem to me to be possible that some different construction might be given to the words of the resolution in that regard. I do not pretend to have considered it very carefully, but I can see some force in the argument of the hon. member for South Lanark. To enter into a contract with a company which is about to construct a dry dock is an entirely different thing from entering into a contract with a company which has already substantially constructed a dock, and there are reasons of public policy why a resolution of this kind should be applicable in one case and not in another. However, this is a matter entirely for the hon. Minister of Finance, and I am only offering this suggestion because I think there may be something in what has been said by my hon. friend from South Lanark. Now, the hon. Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) has spoken of a change of heart. My hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) did not see fit to make any observation upon a change of heart on the part of the hon. Postmaster General. I do not know that it would be necessary for me to remind the hon. Postmaster General of certain changes that he has experienced-

I could also compliment the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) in the same way.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax)-during the last five or six years in regard to matters of public policy. I would almost think that some other member of the government might make observations of that kind rather than the hon. Postmaster General. There is one matter to which I would like to call to the
attention of the hon. Minister of Finance and it is that the resolution in these terms seems to provide for a subsidy to a company which might have no need of any such assistance. I am speaking of this because this resolution does not apply to the Colling-wood docks, but it applies to docks all over Canada, wherever they may be built. As I understand the situation it is impossible for this dock to be proceeded with at Colling-wood without some assistance; nevertheless, we might not have similar conditions elsewhere, and I would point out for the consideration of the hon. Minister of Finance that while this Act is in force you might have conditions somewhere else iii Canada which would enable a company to go on with the construction of a work of this kind as a fair commercial enterprise, yielding a legitimate return and yet the Governor in Council, it seems to me, would be bound to approve of that company. The only thing that seems to be required by the terms of the motion is that the company shall satisfy the government of its ability to perform the work. Such a company as that to which I have referred could abundantly satisfy the government that it would have the ability to perform the work. Would it not be worth while to consider whether or not some amendment might be made in the terms of the resolution in that regard ? It may be that all this has been considered by the hon. Minister of Finance, and that he has some perfectly valid answer to give, but not having heard any answer up to the present time in that regard, I thought it well to bring it to his attention.
Then, there is another matter which I would like to mention. I do not know whether or not the terms of the resolution of 1882 were exactly embodied in the statute which is in force at the present time, but I observe in the concluding part of the resolution which was moved by Sir Leonard Tilley on the 16th May, 1882, this provision :
And further, that these docks shall be free for the use of all vessels and dredges owned by or in the service of the Dominion government.
I do not know whether a provision of that kind has been considered by the government.
So far as the principle of the resolution is concerned I must say that I am in favour of granting this assistance to dry docks and particularly to docks on the great lakes. It should be the object of government in this country of all political parties to build up a great shipping industry on the lakes, to increase our mercantile marine there, and I do not think, so far as my limited information goes, that that can be effectually done unless we have dry docks of sufficient capacity on the lakes to accommodate the vessels of the very large tonnage which are required now in our inland navigation. Therefore, so far as I am concerned, I approve of the principle of the resolution and I hope the dry dock at Col-

ling wood will be completed and that it will be of material assistance in increasing Canadian shipping on the lake.
As far as the question of government by Order in Council is concerned, I have expressed my views in regard to that on more than one occasion in this House. I believe we should have as little government by Order in Council in this country as possible. I also believe that at present we have a little too much of it, as we possibly had before the present government came into power, but I am bound to say, so far as this particular resolution is concerned, that I do not see that the objections which are applicable in some other cases have really very much force. The only function of the Order in Council in this case is to signify approval by the government of the company. That approval is of course in regard to the ability of the company to carry out the work. It is quite right that the government shall not enter into an agreement for assistance to a company that is not able to carry out the work. You must have some tribunal to judge of the company's ability, and I do not see that you can constitute any other tribunal except the government itself for that purpose. Under these circumstances it seems to me, subject to the observations wliich'I have already made, it is a proper resolution to be passed. I trust it will have the effect of stimulating the Canadian shipping industry upon the great lakes.
Hear, hear.

I suppose the government have very carefully considered the raising of the guarantee to 3 per cent. When I had the honour of being a colleague of the Minister of Finance, we made an agreement with the Collingwood Company whereby they undertook to carry out their works for 2 per cent, and they are going on with the work now. The St. John, N.B., Company thought they could get along with the same guarantee of two per cent. They have received a guarantee from the local government and from the city of St. John, but they failed to get the guarantee they expected from the imperial government. The Collingwood Company is building their dock without any guarantee from the town of Collingwood, their only inducement being the two per cent which they are entitled to under the present law. If this Bill passes, of course the Collingwood Company would have the same advantage as other companies would have, but all the same the facts are that the 3 per cent for twenty years will practically cover the total cost of the work. It is a very good guarantee. I do not blame the Minister of Finance ; I am sure he has gone carefully into it, and that he is satisfied himself that with a less guarantee the St. John Dock Company could not go on. The hon. Minister of Finance is a very careful man on matters of this kind.
I grant that cheerfully, and I am sure that he has given a good deal of attention to this matter.

The hon. leader of the opposition in a criticism which is eminently fair, read from some words of the resolution of Sir Leonard Tilley in 1882, from which it would appear that any dock constructed under the provisions of the Act to be founded on the said resolution, should handle the dredges of Canada free of charge. I have not looked up the early history of the matter, but, however, that may be, it is quite evident that the Minister of Finance of that day, for good reasons no doubt, found it better to withdraw this stipulation, and while those words appeared in the original proposal to the House, they were not carried into the resolution or into the Act which was founded on the resolution.
It will still remain a question whether in view of the increased subsidy that is being given now. some such provision should not be inserted in the present resolution.

That is a fair question for discussion, but it would seem that we would be giving the company a subsidy with one hand and to a certain extent taking it back with the other. As to the point, whether in some cases the subsidy of three per cent may not be more than is necessary, we have a provision which will correct that. I propose that the Bill shall provide that the tariff of tolls for the operation of these docks shall be subject to the approval of the Governor General in Council. Experience has shown that it is difficult to raise capital for works of this character, and that such works when first erected are not as a rule profitable. My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) is aware that the Halifax dock was not for years a profitable enterprise. Even yet, I do not know that it is a money-making concern, although I am glad to know that in recent years it is busier than it formerly was. If experience should show in any case that an enterprise would pay more than a fair return to the promoters, we have the remedy in the shape of a reduction in tolls, and in that way the shipping community and all concerned will have the benefit of it. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) will admit that is a fair answer to his criticism.

I would admit to a certain extent it is an answer, except that you might have a company doing an enormous business and paying large dividends, and if the government reduced the tolls in such a case, then at the end of twenty years it might put the company in the embarrassing position, having its tolls reduced once, of undertaking to raise them again.

The usual way is that the subsidy would prob-

ably be converted into cash and would go into the original capital expenditure. It would not affect future transactions. '
That might be, but there still remains the difficulty that if you reduce the tolls the company might be constrained to raise them again at the end of the twenty years.

From the remarks of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) I would infer that it was the intention of the government to grant the increased subsidy of three per cent to the Collingwood Dry Dock, only, because Owen Sound and Midland are not many miles from that point. If that is the case, it would be a great disappointment to the people who own the dry dock at Owen Sound. The dry dock in that town is owned by the North American Bent Chair Company, who operate it, and at the last election in which I was the Conservative candidate, two members of that firm, who hitherto voted Conservative, canvassed their employees to support the government candidate because they expected a large subsidy from the government for the purpose of enlarging that dock. Now, if the hon. member for North Norfolk was inspired in his remarks-he was visited just a moment before he made them by the Postmaster General-I must say it would be a great disappointment to the people of Owen Sound-

I may say, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Thomson) will permit me, that I am not inspired by the government. I was speaking only upon general principles, and I expressed my individual opinion that the dry dock at Collingwood would serve the purposes of the Georgian bay district. I have no objection to a dock being built at Owen Sound. I trust that my friends at Owen Sound will be able to raise the money to build one, and if they do they will get the grant under this resolution.

I did not mention the subject of Owen Sound to my hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) nor was that very important centre in my mind when I made some observations to that gentleman on an entirely different subject.

I am very glad to hear the explanation, but the member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) cannot forget that he said it would be out of place for the government to grant a subsidy to Collingwood, and also to Meaford and Owen Sound, they being so close together.
I said nothing of the kind.
Well, words to that effect.
No, not to that effect even.

I would like to hear the Finance Minister define clearly the policy of the government in this matter. It is a matter of great importance to the constituency from which I come. If these people canvassed the electors in the late by-election on the ground of receiving a large subsidy from the government, and if the government will not grant that subsidy, I would like to know it, and the people of North Grey, especially the people of Owen Sound, would like to know it The town of Collingwood is not the only town that has constructed large vessels plying on the upper lakes. The largest and most palatial of these vessels were constructed at Owen Sound. I refer to the steamship ' Manitoba,' the ferry boat ' Ontario,' which plies across the straits at Detroit, and many other large vessels, including three cruisers which were built for the government of Canada. I would like the Finance Minister to declare specifically whether Owen Sound is to be permitted to participate in these grants. Before I sit down, I wish to congratulate the government on taking this step. I believe it is one in the right direction. For many years Canada, though possessing such a large body of fresh water, has been under such disadvantages for the lack of dry docks that a Canadian vessel of any capacity had to leave her own shores and go to an American port to be repaired. Such a condition of things was not to the credit of Canada, and I am very glad that the government have taken this step to promote the construction of dry docks in this country.

In order to remove any doubt as to whether the Act to be founded on this resolution will apply to a dock now under construction, I propose to insert the words ' dry dock ' in the the fifth line, the words ' or to complete a dry dock in course of construction.'
Would you not also include the enlargement of a dock ?
We have other provisions relating to enlargement, which is a different matter.

I am glad to see that the government are keeping faith with these two ports. The prospectus which has been read is evidence that there was some understanding on this subject, in violation of the constitution. My hon. friend the exMinister of Public Works was quite correct. He says he made an agreement at 2 per cent, and that was going as far as the law permitted. You cannot satisfy the public, nor do I think you can satisfy this House, that that company had not some promise on which they issued their prospectus. They would have no object in making absolute misstatements. It would be equivalent to a fraud to get subscriptions to their stock in that way. We have now legislation enlarg-



mg the scope of the government aid, not to meet a specific case, but generally. Whether Owen Sound will succeed in getting any portion of this aid the future only will tell, because, unfortunately for Owen Sound, my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Thomson) was elected to the opposition benches, notwithstanding this promise, and I am afraid Owen Sound will only receive cold justice, while warm justice will be given to Collingwood. Now, the Act does not go far enough. The hon. Finance Minister is making it broad enough to enable the government to keep faith with Collingwood at any rate, and we shall see what they will do with Owen Sound. But I rose to make a few remarks in reply to my hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). His was an extraordinary speech. Sometimes we think him an extraordinary gentleman, and no doubt he is. He started by congratulating me on my conversion, as he put it, to sound constitutional principles in regard to Orders in Council, and he made quite a long speech justifying the government's departure from those principles in this particular Bill. My hon. friend is on record on this question, as on many others, and he ought to have a better memory than he sometimes displays in dealing with matters of this kind. In regard to Orders in Council, the hon. gentleman said :
The motion that I have put into your hands, Mr. Speaker, refers to a matter of very considerable importance, and to a line of conduct adopted by the government which, in my opinion, is a usurpation of power. The government, of course, must have a majority to sustain them as a government, but the majority should keep the government in its proper place. If it merely fills the functions of a majority and is guilty of slavish submission to the government, and permits the government to usurp the powers that a ministry of a free country ought not to possess, then the majority becomes subservient to the government and recreant to its duty to the people who sent it here. The independence of this House has been seriously impaired in the last few years from various causes, and I think we are gradually drifting into a course of procedure and into a policy in respect of which it is high time we should call a halt, and adopt a policy more in consonance with the principles of free and representative government. In the English colonies on this continent, from almost the time that they were established there was a constant struggle on the part of the people while these were crown colonies against the power exercised by the Governor in Council, and a constant demand made by the people for representative government, the benefits of which, though so highly appreciated by the early colonists, we seem in this Dominion at present to place a lower estimate upon than was placed upon them 150 to 200 years ago. The objections to the system of legislation by Order in Council are numerous.
I could give considerably more, but I will give the bon. gentleman's wind-up.
I wish to point out that in the last eight or nine years the government have, by Order in Council, adopted important fiscal legislation Hon. Mr. TISDALE.
which should not have been adopted without reference to this House.
I think the bon. gentleman's approval of this measure, contrasted with bis speech which I have quoted, justifies me in saying that his speech to-day was an extraordinary speech.

If the hon. gentleman will allow me, I will say that in my speech to-day I have merely taken ground in favour of the expenditure of money which has been already authorized by this House, and the remarks he quotes do not apply to the present occasion.

I will leave the hon. gentleman to be judged by what he said, and I will venture to say that his speech, as reported in the first edition of ' Hansard,' at all events, will bear out my strictures upon him. Just one word with regard to the remark made by the hon. Postmaster Gene- ,, ral, that I had in any way changed my views on the principle of this legislation. I would simply point out that while, in many cases, the expenditure by Order in Council would be a matter of very slight import, where the expenditure involved was comparatively slight, and where it was much more convenient that such expenditure should be dealt with in this way, the question assumes an altogether different complexion when serious expenditure is at stake, and in such case I feel justified in insisting strongly that such, as a practice, is contrary to constitutional principles.
Resolution reported.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
That it is expedient to amend the Customs Act, chapter 32, revised statutes, and to provide as follows :-
1.	That the expression ' duty ' shall include ' surtax.'
2.	That a change be made in the composition of the board of customs, and that an assistant commissioner of customs be appointed ?
3.	That authority be given for the employment of temporary officers of customs.
4.	To better define the powers of the board of customs ?
5.	That further particulars be given in invoices ; and to provide that invoices may be made out in the currency in which the goods are actually purchased.
6.	To define the rate of duty upon unenumerated articles, made of more than one material.
7.	To extend the time for the submission of claims for refund, including claims for refund on account of damage.
8.	That importers may be relieved from the payment of duty on damaged goods, abandoned in certain cases.
9.	That the basis of allowance for damage ou polished steel, and other articles, be changed.
10.	To authorize the granting of relief from the payment of duty on goods, destroyed or damaged while in the custody of the customs.
11.	That further provision be made for the valuation for duty purposes of medicinal and

other preparations, and in respect of the testing of sugars, molasses, wines, spirituous and alcoholic liquors.
12.	To authorize collectors of customs to require further proof in respect of invoices.
13.	To vest in officers the power to administer oaths.
14.	To confer further powers on the Governor in Council respecting special customs services and overtime of officers ; and also respecting the reduction of customs duties on imported goods.-The Minister of Customs.
The first clause has reference to the surtax. This is a new word Introduced into our tariff and customs laws, and it was thought well that it should be defined and included In the term ' duty.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS (Hon. William Paterson).

speechtext: What is the definition of the word ' surtax ' in the dictionary of the free traders ? This is the first time we have had in Canada this expression introduced into our tariff laws. It is one of the most pronounced protectionist words, involving one of the most pronounced protectionist principles, and here we have free traders, who wish for free trade as they have it in England, adopting this expression. Let me offer them my congratulations.
What will be the exact effect of making the word ' duty ' include the word ' surtax ' ?

It would, I presume, be included in any ease, but this puts it beyond doubt. With reference to these changes in the Customs Act, of which I have given notice, I may say that I am bringing forward these amendments, which are not very important, this session, so that they may be included in the consolidation of the Customs laws which is now taking place.
On section 2,

The present board of customs is composed of many of our appraisers, some of whom reside in Victoria, Winipeg, Hamilton, Toronto, Ottawa. Montreal and Halifax. We have occasion at times to call the board together to discuss certain questions, and it may not be convenient, nor may the business be important enough, always to call officers from such distant points. It is proposed to specify that the Commissioner of Customs shall be chairman of the board, and leave to the Governor in Council the naming of such other officers as may be required to act with him and constitute the beard. Of course, new members to the board could be added from time to time. As regards the assistant commissioner, I have already given the reasons, during the discussion on the estimates, why it was thought desirable one should be appointed.
Will the new members of the Board of Customs be members of the civil service ?
They must be.
How is the board constituted at present ?

It is constituted of gentlemen in the different outposts. For instance, at Victoria, I think that the collector is one of the board. At Montreal the appraisers of dry goods and hardware are on it. At Hamilton one of the appraisers is a member, also at Toronto. Mr. Breadner, who is the chief clerk in the department here, is also a member of the board, and one or two of the other officers in the inside department.
What functions do they exercise, as distinguished from those of the Commissioner of Customs himself.?

As lion, gentlemen will understand, questions arise, owing to the changing conditions of business and new lines of goods coming in, in which there will be differences of opinion as to the rate of duty that should be imposed upon a certain article. If these claims are not very pressing, we set them aside until a number of them are awaiting a decision. Then a meeting of the board is held and the members of the board in meeting discuss these matters and arrive at a decision. Opinions not always unanimous, but, as in every case, questions must be decided by a majority. When a decision is reached, it is reported to the Minister of Customs. If the minister approves it and signs it, that ruling of the board of customs has the force of statute law, subject, however, to an appeal to the Governor in Council.

Is it contemplated under this new Act, and with these new appointments to provide, at the large ports-Montreal, Toronto and perhaps some others-appraisers who will understand each a particular line of goods ? At the present time, a single appraiser is supposed to understand hardware business, textile business, grocery business and so on. The difficulty under which we labour in this respect grows more apparent as the country's business increases. I think the business going through these larger ports is sufficient to warrant the government in specializing more than we have done in the past. This is the system followed in the larger ports of the United States. Has the government in contemplation any such step as this ?

Of course, this Bill will not be effective in that way ; it is a matter of departmental arrangement. The question, of course, is one of importance. The objection is largely one of the expense and the multiplication of officers. No doubt it would be more satisfactory if we were able to increase our staff of appraisers, and, perhaps, at some ports where

we have not them, we should have them. But, of course, the expense of the department has increased considerably of late ; and, while we have endeavoured to keep pace with the business, we have hesitated to employ all the officers, or create all the new offices that, perhaps, might be desirable. We intend, to try to keep pace with the requirements of the service. If we find ports where the appraisers are overworked, I think the suggestion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kemp) will have to be given effect to in one or more of the ports before very long.

I think the argument given by the hon. minister will hardly be an excuse for not taking some definite step at an early day. As to the question of ex pense, what the government would sa"ve by levying the duties properly chargeable on goods would more than offset the expenditures involved by the appointment of these officers. If the hon. minister has looked into the system in the larger cities in the United States, he has found appraisers who are to be considered more as specialists than are those of our own country. My own opinion is that each appraiser with us is supposed to be informed with regard to too many lines of business. He can not do justice to all, and, the proper duty not being charged, the revenue is often cheated of what it should fairly receive. I do not see that the consideration of expense should stand in the way of the improvement I have suggested.

The object of the Tariff Act and the appointment of the appraisers is, not only to collect revenue, but to carry out the principle of protection. There is a lack of appraising force in the Customs department, and by reason of this, Canadian manufacturers have been discriminated against. My own attention has been drawn quite recently to a case in which certain machines were brought into a city in Canada at a valuation of $1,000, when further investigation proved that they should have been brought in at a valuation of $1,800. The work of making this change had to be done by the manufacturer who was interested in the business in Canada. He found the American manufacturers sending the machines into Canada, and Canadian appraisers putting' them through the customs at a valuation of little over half of what they were bought for. So, it is not only in the interest of the revenue, but in the interests of the Canadian manufacturer and the Canadian workman that the appraisers should be competent and sufficiently numerous, and that they should be encouraged to perform their duties in the way of protecting the Canadian manufacturer. And in that relation I would like to ask the Minister of Customs whether there is any punishment for the perpetration of acts of this character ?

Section 8 of the Customs law provides that, if articles are undervalued by more than fifteen per cent, double the duty on the undervaluation shall be collected. This section is mandatory. Of course, where fraud is suspected and proven, penalties are levied upon the perpetrators of them. As to machinery coming in under-valued, in some cases second hand machinery is brought in, which may not have a market value. To meet cases of that kind, we added to our staff an agent who was for many years connected with one of the large machine works. If machinery comes in at a port where there is not an appraiser or where we are not satisfied with the valuation of the regular appraiser, it is the duty of this officer to proceed to the port and appraise the article and see that it is entered at proper value. In the larger cities, I think, the appraising is done very fairly. In Toronto, for instance, we have a textile appraiser, a grocery appraiser and a hardware appraiser. These are the principal ones. I grant you that one or other of these departments would have to take in stationery, boots and shoes, and other lines. But, I think, we are pretty well manned in that respect in many ports. In addition, we have the check of the department here. If anything seems wrong, the port is written to and, if necessary, the invoices are called for and an inquiry made ; then, if there has been an under-appraisement, an amended appraisement is made and the amended duty is paid by the importer.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Paterson) has taken power to appoint an assistant commissioner. Is the gentleman who is to be appointed now in the service, or will an outsider be brought hi ?
He is in the service, and has been since 1896.

The hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) has raised the question of penalties for under-valuation. I presume the hon. minister finds a growing tendency to attempt to defraud the customs by undervaluation. I understand that this is not a criminal offence under the Customs Act, as it is under the law of the United States.
It is certainly an offence.
A criminal offence ?

It has never been so dealt with since I came into office. No parties have been proceeded against with a view of having them imprisoned. But they do, no doubt, proceed in that way, and there is generally a money penalty.
Should there not be a clause in the Criminal Code dealing with offences of this kind ?

I think there is power under the Inspection Act to do that. As hon. gentlemen will understand, there are two sides to a question. Sometimes the entry may have an appearance of deliberate fraud, there are cases that look suspicious ; and where there really have been contraventions of the Act penalties have been put upon the offenders. But they put forward their side of the case and claim that they acted in ignorance of the law, that they bought the article for that price, and thought they had a right to enter it at that price. As the hon. gentleman knows, there are export prices ; foreigners, when effecting sales in this country to our own merchants, will quote an export price. Well, that is right enough, the Customs Department cannot interfere with that. If a man in another country wishes to sell his goods at 25 per cent under the domestic price, that is a perfectly legitimate transaction as between the seller and the buyer. But the law makes it imperative on the Customs Department to see that the duty is paid on the value of that article in the country of production, and that law we endeavour to carry out.

Representations have been made to the Minister of Customs with respect to making the law more stringent with regard to undervaluation, and it has been proposed to adopt some clauses of the law in force in the United States. Is not that the case ?

Yes, there was a suggestion in some of the Toronto papers, I think it was in the ' Toronto News,' that we should adopt the practice of the United States in fixing the value for duty. Well, I think the writer of that article is under a mistake. The United States law is virtually the same as ours, it takes the value of the goods in the country from whence they are exported and levies the duty upon that value. It is the same in the United States, as it is with us in that respect. I do not know that you could fix any other standard. I have thought the matter over a good deal as to what should form the standard, say of the Canadian value. How would you determine the Canadian value of an article ? I think the fairest way is that when an article Is sold in the country of production you get an affidavit from the seller, and at present as hon. gentlemen know we do not require such affidavit, it is something that we put in operation since I took charge of the department. But previous to that, all the exporter had to do was to certify his invoice as correct. Well, he sold goods, we will say, 20 per cent less than they were sold in the country of production, but the transaction was correct as between the two individuals, the buyer actually bought them for that money, but that was not the value at which they should be entered for duty.
So the importer here would say, when he was called upon for an amended entry. Well, I did not know what the value was, the drummer told me that was the price. Well, the man who sells the goods knows, and we will oblige him to make a declaration on his invoice that the price appearing on the invoice is the price at which the goods are sold in the country from whence they are exported ; and when there is any advance, then that is noted upon the invoice. Say an article was charged at $1.00 and the selling price was $1.25 ; the difference is noted, and the entry is made upon $1.25 instead of $1.00.
At six o'clock Committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
On section 2,

I assume at the present time, from the wording of this resolution, that there is no assistant commissioner. I notice by the Customs Act, chapter 32, of the Revised Statutes, that authority is given there to appoint an assistant commissioner. Why repeat it in the proposed amendment ?

There is no authority in the present Customs Act, as we have it, for the appointment of an assistant commissioner. There was an assistant commissioner a few years ago, but I think that was changed in 1S94, or perhaps before that. There is no provision in the present Act for the appointment of an assistant commissioner, and so we propose it now.

I find, referring to chapter 32, which the hon. minister proposes to amend, that clause 4 says :
There shall be a commissioner of customs who shall be the deputy of the Minister of Customs and an assistant commissioner.
I presume, from what the hon. gentleman new tells us, that the clause has been amended subsequent to the revision of the statutes.
Yes, and the assistant commissioner has been dropped.

The hon. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson), before the committee rose at six o'clock, was discussing the question of undervaluation. What I said that brought forth these observations was not in reference to the policy that had been promulgated, I think he said in the ' News.' I do not know what the policy was. I hardly know what it had reference to. What I was trying to impress upon the hon. minister was the fact that in our laws in regard to undervaluation, I have been informed, there is no such thing as

a penal offence. There are money penalties, but there are no penal offences such as exist under the customs laws of the United States. I was under the impression that representations had been made to the government-I do not know whether they came under the observation of the lion. Minister of Customs or of some of his colleagues-recommending that the American law be considered, and that in such cases as it is practicable, the provisions in relation to undervaluation be embodied in our law. I do not see anything in these amendments looking in that direction. The hon. Minister of Customs said that because of the facilities for preventing undervaluation and fraud upon the revenue in the larger cities, undervaluation was not likely to take place in the larger cities to as great an extent ns in the smaller towns, and that brings forward a very important matter. I, for myself, do not see that it is possible to have goods valued or to know whether the invoices represent the proper value at any of the smaller ports. I do not know how this thing is regulated in other countries, but I do know that in this country it is often said that when an invoice for goods is presented at an outlying place, it is likely to go through with greater facility than if the goods are passed through customs at a larger place. Of course, the hon. Minister of Customs has said that each invoice is reviewed by the department when it reaches Ottawa, but it is almost impossible to tell without being able to examine the goods and make a proper comparison, whether the valuation has been proper or not. The officers in these smaller places have not the information before them; they have not the price lists and necessary data. I think perhaps we have too many ports of entry, and that there are too many small places where facilities of that kind are given, and that, consequently, a great deal of fraud must result. I do not know whether the hon. minister has ever thought of making any changes in respect to the administration of the customs of this country that would obviate that kind of thing.
There is this difficulty; in the United States I think they have no more ports of entry than we have in Canada.
In the whole of the United States ?
I do not mean proportionately. I think that, perhaps, in the whole of the United States, they have no more ports of entry than wTe have in Canada.

That is what I understand.
_ The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS. Repre-
' sentations have been made to me by merchants in the larger places that it would be in the interest of the community if we Mr. KEMP.
had a less number of these smaller ports, and if the ports of entry were more concentrated. Well, there is that aspect of the case ; there is no doubt about that. We do get a better examination of goods, but the difficulty we experience in reference to that is that the smaller iffaces are asking for the convenience of customs officers, and the pressure upon the department was never greater than at the present time for more ports. I think that I have at present applications from perhaps twenty places now for customs facilities. They represent that they are many miles away from a customs port, and that they cannot receive their goods without going backward and forward and thus they are making out a very strong case. I cannot very well see that you can refuse one section of the community the facilities that are given to another within proper, reasonable bounds. To say that persons living conveniently, perhaps, to one of our larger places shall enjoy customs facilities, while others living at a greater distance and who are contributing to the revenue too shall not have the same conveniences is what presents the difficulty in not only attempting to close small ports, but in dealing with applications for new ports to be created. It would be a very difficult matter indeed after a place is once established as a customs port, even where the business would not warrant it, ns far as the revenue is concerned and where the revenue actually will be perhaps 50 per cent of the sum required for the payment of the expense attendant upon its collection, to close such a port. All we have been able to do is-shall I say to resist the pressure as far as we can from other places in order that we should not increase the number of ports immoderately. Where you have ports now existing, where the revenue is a certain amount and where another place of equal importance and of equal revenue presents its claim to have customs facilities it is rather difficult to answer a request of that kind. The convenience of the public must, in a measure, be sought. It is accompanied with the disadvantage that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kemp) has alluded to, and which we use as an argument when we are presenting the difficulties to those who are pressing for additional customs ports. It is one of the arguments that we have to make use of that we have better facilities for the examination of goods and determining what the proper value and rate of duty are at the larger places where we have competent officers. I have no doubt that the collector does his best to carry out the law, but in many of these smaller ports we have only the collector. He has to be the appraiser, he has to do the whole of the work, and he will do it to the best of his ability. However, there are no very heavy importations at these ports, and I think, taking it all in all, that perhaps no very serious charge can be made that the revenue is

suffering or that other traders whose interests must he considered as well as the collection of the revenue are put under any serious disadvantage. Of course, you can understand that if at one port goods can be entered at a lower rate of duty, or that the proper valuation is not scrutinized as well as at another, those doing business at a port with a more efficient administration would be at a disadvautgae as against those who were importing their goods through the other port. I quite recognize that, but all invoices are scrutinized by the check department in the city of Ottawa.
Suppose an invoice is presented to a customs-house officer at a small point, is he the absolute judge as to the classification under which these goods shall pass the custom-house ?

Yes, he takes the entry and passes it to the best of his knowledge. All these entries at the large ports as well as the small ports come to the headquarters here, and they are scrutinized by the check department, but in the first instance, the collector has of necessity to make the entry, and he has to do it to* the best of his judgment as to his duty under the circumstances.
Mr. BLA1N. There is very considerable dissatisfaction in the commercial world with regard to the value for duty placed on certain articles. I am informed by one of the leading scale manufacturers in Toronto, that in the case of certain registering scales imported from the United States which are sold retail in Canada for $60 or $70 each, thev are valued for duty at only $0 or $7 each. The American manufacturer seeing that there is a market in Canada for a new article which is not made in Canada, invoices it from himself in the United States to himself in Canada at a low rate, and as in the case of the scales I have mentioned the difference between the value for duty and the price at which they are sold to the public is out of all proportion. Has this matter been brought to the attention of the Minister of Customs ?

The question as to the proper value for scales has been before the department several times, but I do not know that the particular scale to which the hon. gentleman has referred has been under consideration. We have officers in the United States whose duty it is to ascertain the value of articles in. that country. We have not such officers in Great Britain or on the continent. The officers in the United States go to headquarters and ascertain the value from an actual inspection of the books, and the manufacturers in their own interests, wishing to have no trouble with the customshouse when they send goods to Canada, are anxious to afford our officers all proper information in that connection. Our officers satisfy themselves as to the price at
which that article is sold in the United States, and when it comes into Canada iu like quantity and in like condition, no matter what the invoice may say, the duty is levied upon the value of the article as sold in the United States.

Are there any means by which the public can know the rate for duty that is fixed on an article ? I may state to the minister that during last winter, in the business with which I am connected, we had on two different occasions two different sets of invoices sent to us. It is, I suppose, needless to say that that was not done at our request. However, what is supposed to be a reputable business house in the United States sent us one invoice, being the price we were to pay, and another invoice being the price on which we were supposed to pay duty. We sent back the lower invoice which was the only invoice which had the certificate on it. This incident would go to show that such a practice is quite common. I may say also that the agent of a large manufacturing concern in Canton, Ohio, called on me and desired me to import a large quantity of goods, and in giving me his estimate of price he calculated the duty at just one-lialf of what we were supposed to pay f.o.b. at Canton. I asked him if that was his way of doing business and he said that it was. If that be so, and if other firms are doing the same thing, it would appear to be conducted on a fairly large scale. If the public knew the rate at which these articles were valued by the customs, I believe that the publicity would tend to prevent such things occurring.

I may say that we bring in carbons from the United States which are made in Cleveland, and when these carbons come to us the officer collects from us the duty on the price which these carbons are wholesaled for in the United States, no matter what the invoice may say.

The matter alluded to by the hon. member (Mr. La veil) would be a case of fraud, and if that came to our knowledge we would deal severely with any house which practiced it. The forwarding of the two invoices would be a fraud upon the revenue, and it would be a serious matter for that house if they were detected.

The point I wish to make is. that it appears to be a common practice. We declined to have any business dealings with the house whose agent suggested the lower rate for customs duty to us, and we have not sent any further orders to the man who sent us the duplicate invoices. It would appear from their representations to us. that it is a very common thing for them to do. I am sorry I did not send the duplicate invoices to the minister.

We are very pleased whenever any one gives us

information that will enable us to detect frauds of that kind, and of course we do not divulge the names of those giving us the Information. Whenever a matter of that kind comes to our knowledge you may depend upon it that it is followed up, and penalties imposed that would effectually prevent its recurrence so far as that house was concerned. If a man sold a bill of goods to this country and sent a fraudulent invoice, I' question if he could collect the amount at all in Canada.

I am afraid I did not make, myself clear with reference to the duty on carbons to which I have referred. We buy these earbons in the United States for SS a thousand, but as they are sold to dealers in the United States for $9 a thousand, we have to pay duty on them at the rate of $9, although we only pay $8.

If these articles were presented at an outport of customs and the officer was not familiar with the value, the invoice for $8 per thousand would be the price on which the duty would be assessed. If it was afterwards shown that these goods were sold in the United States at $9, it is possible the department would take some action, but in the meantime the goods would have found their way into Canada on the valuation of $8 per thousand.

If I understand the hon. gentleman from Renfrew (Mr. Wright) he rather complains that while he only pays $8 per thousand, we make him pay duty on $9 per thousand. Sometimes we receive complaints of that kind. Parliament determines what the duty should be, and we carry it out. It is our duty under the law to collect the revenue that properly accrues. If an entry of the kind referred to by hon. friend for Peel were made at one of the smaller ports, the only check we have is that a copy of the entry has to come to Ottawa, where it is examined by our checking department. I do not say that we detect everything, but if an entry of a certain class of goods came in at a different price from that prevailing at other and larger ports, the officer would immediately call for an amended entry.

When I first mentioned this matter I asked if there was any way in which the public could find out the value fixed by the department upon certain standard goods. If this information could be obtained, it would be easy to head off many of these frauds.

When decisions are given by the department on certain questions that may not be plain, circulars are sent out to the different collectors, conveying the information. In the great majority of cases the collectors themselves will know what valuation to place upon regular articles of merchandise which have a known market value. There may be Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
special cases in which they would not know. In these cases we avail ourselves of the safe-guard provided by our checking department ; and if an entry comes in which has been undervalued and an amended entry is called for, that would be a guide for the collector in the future. In addition to that, there are trade journals which are made use of, such as the ' Iron Age,' as guides for ascertaining correct valuations.

Is there any way in which one business man can find out the figure at which goods are being imported by others ? Take, for example, a certain class of carriage, which is well known in the. trade. It is purchased at a certain price, but is invoiced at below that price. One dealer might accept that invoice and another might refuse it. Is there any way in which a person importing these goods or the general public can get information as to their valuation from the Customs Department ?

Of course, the Customs Department is not at liberty to reveal to the general public any invoices or values ; but the officers themselves are supposed to know the values, and to be able to tell the importer, when he comes to make his entry, what the proper value for duty should be. Further than that I do not know that we can go.

I wish to ask the minister if within recent months any specific charges have been placed before him in relation to the improper or fraudulent importation of German goods under the British preference. The reason I ask this is that during the famous tour of the leader of the opposition and his party of friends through the west last fall, members of his party made charges throughout the country-one member in particular, I think it was the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain)-at various public meetings, which charges by inference or implication meant that certain citizens of the North-west Territories had been guilty of fraud in bringing into Canada German goods under the British preference.

I may say that the hon. member for West Assiniboia is quite correct when he says that the party travelling in the west last year with the hon. leader of tlie oposition made the charges against the government that German goods "were brought into this country under the British preference. That would not be news to this House, for the hon. member for West Toronto, when discussing the matter at the last session, showed this House, and his statement went uncontradicted, that a large quantity of German goods were imported from time to time into the country. The hon. member for West Assiniboia has made a statement that is very wide in its character, to the effect that some members of the party made this charge at every place in

western Canada. That Is not true. I may say that I made reference to it at one point in the west, though it could have been truthfully made at every meeting, because it was well understood. The charge has been made by the Liberal-Conservative party in this House, that German goods were brought into this country under the guise of the British preference. The government, endorsed by the hon. member for West Assiniboia, said that was not correct ; but what is the condition of things to-day ? The government at this session of parliament give notice to the world that they would abolish the preference. WTiy are' we discussing this item now ? For the reason that we are going to place in the customs tariff of this country a surtax specially directed against German goods. Now, it is very well understood that the Speaker, or Chairman, has not to sit down when an hon. member gets up whether the Speaker, or Chairman, is in order or not. The rule is that an hon. member must sit down until the point of order is decided. That is the rule and that is the procedure of parliament.

I must object to your ruling, Mr. Chairman. Every member of this House has a right to discuss a question of order before the Chair decides it, and we have an appeal from the chairman, thank goodness, to the Speaker of the House. We can at any time ask you, Mr. Chairman, to vacate the chair and ask the Speaker to come in and decide a question of order. I intend to speak to the question of order. The hon. Minister of Finance is perfectly right when he states that any member is required when he quotes from a public document to put it on the Table of the House. No member of the House has the right to quote even an affidavit, or a writing, or an article from a newspaper, when a question is discussed in the House, attacking the integrity of an hon. member of the House when the hon. member denies it. The point was decided some years ago. Sir Charles Tupper made a statement in this House and an hon. member produced an affidavit to deny it. The Speaker ruled that no affidavit or statement made by any man outside of the House could be read in the House for that purpose. Now, the chairman of this committee seeks to override that well established rule of the House. He has drawn a distinction between statements made outside of the House and statements made inside the House. There is no such distinction. A member has a perfect right to make a statement outside the House, and there is no right on the part of any member to bring in an affidavit or written document or newspaper quotation, to show that a statement made by an hon. member inside the House or outside the House is false.

One of the most important things in connection with our customs system is that there should be uniformity of valuation, and the minister has taken steps to attain that as nearly as possible 'by getting the customs appraisers to meet from time to time and make uniform rulings. I must say that in the province of Ontario, and I think in Canada generally, we have very little fault to find with the administration of our custom affairs at the present time. Under the management of the present minister (Hon. Mr. Paterson) we have had very little fault to find indeed.
Hear, hear.
I am afraid, however, that the principal difficulties of the Minister of Customs, come from liis own friends who try to turn everything they can to political account.
Hear, hear.

Apropos of this, I notice that a Bill has been introduced by a gentleman who has made himself very conspicuous this evening. It is an Act to Regulate the Sales and Provide for the Inspection of Textile Fabrics. I have not seen the Bill, but I am told that it requires that all tex-Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
tile goods shall have stamped on them what they are made of. After an experience of fifty years in the textile fabrics business, I may say that I do not believe it is possible to get persons sufficiently well posted to enable them with any degree of certainty to put such a stamp on the goods manufactured in this country alone. This Bill is introduced by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Scott). Now, Sir, if there is any one thing we should expect from our great west, it is that the members who represent that country in the House should be somewhat commensurate in their ideas with the broadness of the magnificent country from which they come. If there is any place from which we could expect largeness and broadness, it is from the North-west, and to have such a matter introduced to this House as was introduced this evening by a gentleman coming from the west, is rather disappointing. I think his constituents should take charge of him when he goes home, and keep him there because his conduct here is not provocative of the best feeling. He has succeeded in creating a very serious difficulty for our worthy chairman whose decisions, as a rule, we are very anxious to support in every way. When we come to consider this Bill introduced by the hon. member, I hope the Minister of Customs will be a little careful about it. because he will find that if he allows it to pass he will require to double the number of the employees who are at present dealing with textile fabrics, and I do not think that is desirable. I make these remarks having noticed that this gentleman from the North-west has introduced this very unpleasant matter this evening, although it is much more unpleasant for himself than for any member on this side of the House. I contend that he having introduced a matter of this kind, and brought into this House such discord and unpleasantness, we will have to review this Bill with a great deal of care, because I have not the least doubt that he may find himself confronted some day with some very serious affidavits from his country, whereby he could probably find a hole in the armour of even the Minister of Customs.

On the question of Order, I wish to have it decided by ihe Speaker of the House. I rose for the purpose of discussing a question of Order and you, Mr. Chairman, rose and you said that when Order was called I had no right to make any observation on the subject. Further than that you made a ruling which I think is contrary to the rights and privileges of members of this House. I ask that yon vacate the Chair and ask the Speaker to come in for the purpose of deciding the point of Order which I intend to discuss before Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I wish to state what is the rule of the House. The Chairman decides all questions and from his decision an appeal can be made to the

committee, but no appeal can be made to tbe Speaker of the House to decide that question of order. But if a question of order should arise, and it is required to censure a particular member for violation of order, that censure cannot be given by the Chairman, but must be referred to the Speaker. That is the difference between the powers of the Speaker and the powers of the Chairman. This committee cannot refer my ruling to the Speaker. The Speaker has no more power to rule on anything that may arise in the committee than I have, when he is in the Chair, to rule on a matter that may arise in the House. Let me read rule 70 :
Questions of order arising in Committee of the Whole House shall he decided by the Chairman, subject to an appeal to the House ; but disorder in a committee can only be censured by the House, on receiving a report thereof.

Might I suggest to my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) that we have really passed from that ques tion to other matters. The point of difference between the hon. member and the Chairman was that the hon. member continued to stand on his feet while the Chairman was on his feet. Clearly the hon. member should have resumed his seat. That is the only point of difference. We have passed from that now, however, and no appeal was taken at the time, and I rather think we had better let the matter drop, especially as the documents have been sent to my hon. friend from Peel.

My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has hardly grasped the point. The point made by my hon. friend from Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) is this : A question of order was raised which required to be decided by the Chair. My hon. friend from Lanark rose to discuss the question. The Chairman rose to give what practically amounted to a decision upon it. The contention of my hon. friend from Lanark, which I think is well founded, is this, that the Chairman has no right to prevent any member from discussing a question of order. He cannot stop discussion on a question of order. Every member of the House has the right to express his opinion on that question, and after every one who desires to speak upon it has spoken, then and not till then is the Chairman to decide the question. Perhaps the Chairman did not understand the situation. If he did, I would not be inclined to agree with his ruling, because I do not know of any rule of this House which prevents any member of the committee from fully discussing the question of order before the Chairman gives his decision. This is the whole question, and perhaps, as my hon. friend the Minister of Finance suggests, my hon. friend from Lanark has no objection now to let the matter rest. However, I will not interfere.

The Chairman of the committee has read the rule of the House in which there is no appeal from the Chairman but to the committee. I do not think that appeal would avail much; but I have very strong opinions on the subject. I have seen this question very often decided in this House. I have again and again seen appeals from the Chairman of the committee to the Speaker of the House, and I have again and again seen the Speaker called in for the purpose of deciding the question. I have often heard the rule laid down in this House that where an hon. gentleman contradicts a statement made by a member, no matter what the opinion of the House may be, no matter what affidavits or quotations from the public press he has in support of that contradiction;' he has been refused the right to read those quotations or affidavits.

I do not propose to occupy very much of the time of the House on this small question which has been introduced by a small representative from the west. There is another small representative who is interrupting me who has a record, lie had better take care of those things that crawl oil him. I may say that I do not propose to make any personal references in this House; that is not my mission here; but I will not allow insinuations to come from the other side of the House without giving an answer to those who interrupt me. The only question of difference seems to be as to whether goods from Germany have been brought into this country under the British preference. Before I proceed to say something on the question, I wish to state that during the western trip I had the honour of being present at one meeting, and one meeting only, in the town of Morden, at which I exhibited the teapot which my hon. friend said was carried up and down all through western Canada. I make that statement on the floor of the House, knowing my responsibility; and when the hon. member for West Assiniboia comes down with letters written by himself, trying to get information from gentlemen in the west to prove anything to the contrary
I beg to call the hon. gentleman to order. On what basis does he say that this letter was prepared by me ?
You said yourself that you prepared it.
I said no such thing.
I may have misunderstood the hon. gentleman, but I certainly understood him to say that he had perhaps written it himself.
I made no such statement. I stated that the letter was given to me at my suggestion, as the reading of it certainly shows.

You wrote to him and got the letter back. X said the hon. gentleman was seeking to get information from the west in respect to statements X made during the western trip in respect to the German teapot which I exhibited at Morden. Let us read the letter and see if this is correct or not:
Walter Scott, Esq., M.P.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your communication.
How did this letter come into the hon. gentleman's hands at all ? Was it offered to the hon. gentleman In order to give him information about some statements that I had made ? Not at all; the hon. gentleman sought it by writing a letter to this gentleman.
It must be perfectly plain to the House that there is a very great difference between a letter being sent to me at my suggestion and my preparing a letter.
There was a telegram among these documents. Did the hon. gentleman take it out before sending the documents over ?
Yes.
I thought you did; just like what the hon. gentleman would do, of course the House would not expect anything else.
Mr. Chairman, these are not questions of order.
The hon. gentleman asked me respecting a telegram. It was either a copy of a telegram sent by me to the gentleman at Morden or one sent by him to me.
We need not thank the hon. gentleman for placing the documents on the Table. He absolutely refused to do so.
I beg your pardon; I did not.
I do not beg any pardon about it. I know what I am stating. Why was the question of placing the documents on the Table raised at all, if you did not refuse to place them on the Table ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The order in discussion is this, that the hon. member who has the floor need not permit, against his will, any 'obstruction or any question during the time he has the floor, except a question of order or a question of privilege.
Is it open to me to raise a point of order ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Of course, a point of order can be raised; but if it is against the will of the hon. gentleman who has the floor, no interruption can take place except on a question of order or a question of privilege.
I raise the point of order, that the hon. gentleman is misrepresenting me. I said before, and I say now, that I did not refuse to place the documents on the Table.

I ask the hon. gentleman to state his point of order, and it will be answered. He is not going to keep the floor all night. I was just going to remark that the committee does not thank the hon. gentleman for laying these documents on the Table, because he refused to lay them on the Table, and refused to send them across for my inspection. I have to thank the hon. Minister of Customs, who, turning around, said to the hon. gentleman ; ' Lay them on the Table.'
You are mistaken.
I will leave it to the hon. Minister of Customs if he did not say that. I heard it, and I call upon him to say whether that is correct or not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The rule is that if a statement is said to have been made by an hon. member, and he rises and says that he did not make that statement, his denial must be accepted there and then.
I rise to discuss that ruling.

Mr. Chairman, will you allow me ? In this case the statement was not attributed to the hon. member for West Assiniboia, and although he denies it, he had no authority to deny it. It was attributed to the hon. Minister of Customs, and the hon. member for Assiniboia had no right whatever to deny it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understood the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) to have said that the hon. member for Assiniboia had made a certain statement and that that hon. gentleman had denied having made it.
No, it was the hon. Minister of Customs who made it.

I understand the rule to be that when an hon. member in this House makes a statement concerning another hon. member but does not make that statement of his own personal knowledge, then he must accept the denial of the hon. member, and withdraw it. But when he makes a statement of his own knowledge concerning another hon. member, there is no rule to make him retract that statement.

The hon. member for Assiniboia was asked to lay on the Table the documents he had read, and he refused to do so. The point of order was raised, and the Chairman of the committee read the rule from the book. But I repeat that the hon. Minister of Customs turned in his place and said to the hon. gentleman :	' Lay
them on the Table.' I leave to the hon. Min-

ister of Customs to say whether that is correct or not.
This is the biggest tempest in a teapot I have ever witnessed.

A discussion having arisen as to whether the hou. member was compelled to lay the papers upon the Table, it was pointed out that if a minister had quoted from a public document, he could be required to lay it upon the Table, but that this rule did not apply to a private member. I then turned around in my seat, and the bon. member for Assin-iboia said to me : ' I have no objection to give them the papers,' and then I said to him : ' Lay them on the Table.'

In view of this statement will the hon. gentleman now apologize to the committee and to myself for having denied the statement I made that the Minister of Customs had turned to him and told him to lay the documents on the Table ? The hon. member for Assiniboia denied this, and said that the hon. Minister of Customs had done nothing of the kind. In the face of this contradiction by the Minister of Customs of the statement made by the hon. member for Assiniboia, how can we believe anything which that hon. gentleman may say ? This document looks as if it had been mutilated, for here is the corner of a telegram which the hon. gentleman acknowledged having torn off. He made a charge against me in his place, and when called on by the Chairman to lay the documents on the Table, instead of complying with that order, as he should have done, he tears off a part of the document and now acknowledges having done so. However, I do not propose taking up any more of the time of the committee on this point. But the contention between the hon. gentleman and myself is this : He says that I travelled up and down the country producing a certain teapot and making certain statements at every meeting I attended in the west.
