I repeat that at no meeting, out of the forty-five held by the hon. leader of the opposition, was that teapot presented except at one, and I challenge the hon. gentleman, or any of his friends to gainsay that statement. The meeting I refer to was held at Morden, and it does look as if the hon. gentleman were a little worried about the German goods and the tariff. During the last few years he has been pointing out in his newspaper to the western people that this government should be supported because it introduced the preferential tariff, and the consumers in the west were getting great advantages from it. Now he applauds the government because it has given notice that it will abolish that preference, and the consumer in the west will no longer have the benefit of it in the case of these goods. To show how much the merchant knew whether 97*
i	*	[DOT]
these goods came in under the preferential tariff at a low or a high valuation, let me refer to what he said himself over Ms own signature. It was in Regina, I think, that I purchased the teapot in question.
I went into a store there and asked the clerk if he sold German goods. He said, yes, we have some, a package up stairs that are not yet opened. I asked him : will you be good enough to sell me an article from one of these packages, and he replied that of course he would. I went upstairs With him, and he opened one of the packages. The first article he took from the box was this teapot. I said :	* That will do,
come down stairs and I will pay you.' I went with him to the office and he produced the original invoice. I never made the statement that the invoice whs for $100, and the hon. gentleman has no right to say that I did. What I did was simply to give as an illustration the $100 item I mentioned, and not the amount of the invoice at all.
I think the invoice was for more than $300. To show how little these people know about how these goods come into this country, let us see what they say in their letter to the hon. gentleman, by which the hon. gentleman was going to prove that these goods did not come in under the preferential tariff at all. They say : 'We have nothing to do with the payment of duties whatever. We did not know what duty was to be paid.' The hon. gentleman has produced a declaration from a gentleman with . whom we had a good deal of trouble in the west, and perhaps he will be good enough to communicate this to that gentleman, either when he goes home or in his newspaper, or by letter, or .send him the telegram which he tore off this lot of papers, or a copy of it. Will he be good enough to inform this Mr. Trant-a government official forsooth, as well-that when private citizens are travelling through the west, he should not crowd himself into their private car and beat his way through as a newspaper reporter ? He is a newspaper man like the hon. gentleman himself, so he will know how this goes. Perhaps he was a writer for the hon. gentleman's own newspaper. Will the hon. gentleman say whether he wrote the report for his own newspaper ?
He did not.
He was too boozy.

That is right-a very proper statement; but I am not making it. Now, this is a long letter, but there is nothing in it, and I regret that the time of the committee is taken up with the matter at all. What I say is that the Liberal-Conservative party contended in this House and in the country that the British preference, so-called, was not a British preference in fact, that it allowed German goods to come into Great Britain and, after a small amount of labour had been put upon them, very

often in the shape of labels and boxes, they were then shipped to Canada under the guise of British goods and allowed to come in under the preference of 33J per cent. The hon. leader of the Liberal-Conservative party, in addressing the House, made the statement that that traffic was actually going on. And I heard the Finance Minister in his place in this House say that this was a matter that should be investigated. Neither the Minister of Finance nor the Minister of Customs was ready to stand up in his place in the House and deny the statement made by the hon. leader of the opposition. And that statement so made was not denied, I repeated in the west, and I repeat it here-that, so far as the British preference allowed German goods to come into this country, we were opposed to it. That is all that the Liberal-Conservative party said. The government declared that the preference was all right. But this year the Finance Minister stated in his place, and gave notice to the Canadian people, that German goods would be retaliated against, that this country could not allow these goods to come in except on the payment of twenty-five per cent higher duty than the general tariff. I do not think it is worth while to say anything further on the teapot question. I bought a razor out there. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) stated that, and it was so.
I did not say so.
Did not the hon. gentleman say so ?
I read it.
And is not the hon. gentleman responsible for what he reads ?
Address the Chair.

' Address the Chair,' says the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt). Perhaps he will be good enough to address the Chair when he is interrupting me. What I say is that I purchased the razor referred to. It was made in Germany. Did the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) make the statement that they were not German goods? They were German goods ; the label was upon the article itself, both upon the teapot and upon the razor. This kind of goods brought in under the so-called British preference to compete with the Canadian goods. I have this to say-and it is more than the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) can say witli reference to the tariff-that the Liberal-Conservative party has taken one stand upon the tariff question, and that we should have one policy, a national policy for the maintenance of Canadian interest, not to allow German goods to come in to compete with Canadian goods. We have taken that stand under our honoured leader in this House. And what we say inside this House we say outside of it. And, as a humble supporter of the Conservative party, I make Mr. BLAIN.
the same statement everywhere, and advocate the national policy everywhere. I am very glad to know that in the discussion that has taken place within the last few years the government has been converted, and that under its recent action these German goods will not have the opportunity of coming in except upon the payment of much higher than the ordinary duty.

Before this tempest in a teapot is over I would like to say a few words on this subject of German goods. I have been an importer for twenty-five years, importing goods both from Germany and from Great Britain, and I think I can tell the House something about the procedure in the importation of these German goods. A traveller comes and takes our order for whatever German goods we want. He guarantees us prices delivered in Montreal, duty paid. The goods are packed in Germany and brought out in the original packages to Montreal. The invoice is made out and the goods are shipped to us. The duty is paid in Montreal-we have nothing to do with paying the duty. Let it be clearly understood that these goods are sent in the original packages and some direct from a German port, the packages being marked on the outside ' Made in Germany,' each package also bearing the name of the place of shipment. How, then, can they go over to England and there be repacked and be brought in here under the preference. It is utterly impossible for anything of that kind to be done. Besides, the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) says these articles are all stamped with the maker's name, or with a ticket placed upon them * Made in Germany.' Take, for instance, a razor. Suppose it to be one of Bokers' razors-the name of the maker is stamped on the blade near the shank. How can that go over to England and have anything done to make it appear as a British product ?
I will tell the hon. gentle man, as he does not know.

I can tell the committee how it is not done. It is utterly impossible for the goods to go to England and then have anything done to them, and to be shipped here as British goods, because, as I say, not only are they stamped ' Made in Germany ' but they come here in the original packages and the name of the maker is stamped on every article-whether it be a razor, a pair of skates or practically anything else. The teapot to which the hon. gentleman referred, he tells us had a ticket on it with the words ' Made in Germany.' How is anybody to contend that goods thus stamped can be put forward as British goods ? This point came up last year, and some of these hon. gentlemen undertook to tell us in dollars and cents the amount of German goods that went into England, and were afterwards shipped here under the preference. The hon. member for East

Toronto (Mr. Kemp) gave the exact amount. But I brought him to task by asking him bow be knew. Let me quote from ' Hansard ' just wbat took place :
How does the hon. gentleman ascertain the amount of goods imported from England that have been partially made in Germany ?

I am making an estimate.
Now, all this talk that goes on is estimate or is based on estimate. Why. any boy ten years old can make estimates, and I think that almost any boy could estimate a good deal better than the hon. member for East Toronto. It is utterly impossible that these goods shipped to us in the original German packages can come in as British goods.

Let me explain just that one point. I asked the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wright) to be good enough to give us an explanation, but he has not done it. I would point out to the committee how this is done. First, the razor has a bone or ivory handle, chiefly a bone handle. Then is added to it a small quantity of steel; that bone and steel are both furnished in Germany. Then the article is made and shaped in Germany, and what my hon. friend refers to is' put on in Germany. After that is done, it represents three-fourths of the value of the article. The article is then shipped over into Sheffield and polished and boxed up, and sent into this country under the British preference. Is not that a German preference ? The bone, the handle, the steel, the shaping is all done in a foreign country, and then they come over and receive a little finishing in Great Britain, and after that is done, they are invoiced under this so-called British preference, and are permitted to come to this country under the guise of the preference as British goods, when there are three-fourths of them German-made.
Mr. "WRIGHT. I would ask how the hon. gentleman knows that that razor was ever in England at all ? It is impossible for him or any other man to tell that.

The point made by the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Wright) must be clear to every person, that is, that goods marked ' made in Germany ' brought to New York, from New York to the port of Montreal, and then taken up to the North-west Territories, certainly came under the general tariff. Now, where is the possibility or likelihood of fraud ? Does not the whole evidence trend the other way ? It is at least as good as proved that there was no fraud attempted, and that these German goods, a sample of which my hon. friend bought from the merchant at Regina marked ' made in Germany,' which came into the country in a large box, that box stamped in large letters ' made in Germany,' or ' German '-I say it is ns good as proved, at all events, that no fraud was attempted and that the proper rate of duty was paid.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman could tell us what rate of duty was paid upon this invoice of three hundred odd dollars' worth of goods that were brought into a hardware store in his own town. Because he is attempting to enlighten the committee upon this question, perhaps he would be good enough to tell us what rate of duty was paid upon them, and whether they went to Great Britain or not 5
I am not able to tell that.
I thought not.

The merchant was not able to tell me, and the editor of the Morden ' Chronicle ' swears to the accuracy of his report, stating that my hon. friend said the Regina merchant told him what the merchant says he did not know and did not tell.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if that letter does not say distinctly that these goods came to Regina in the original package, and that the words ' from Germany ' were on the outside of the package ?
Yes.
Then it would be impossible for any collector of customs to pass these goods.

Practically impossible. Therefore the argument of the hon. member for Peel had no point. Notwithstanding the various reports that appeared in the Northwest newspapers, notwithstanding the statements made by my hon. friend as appears by this statutory declaration, it is plain that the goods came in under the general rate of duty. I do not know the rate of duty, but I would like to know it, and I will give the information to the Minister of Customs, which may enable him to know. The goods came in seven cases, numbered from 4364 to 4370. They were received at Regina on September 2. The Minister of Customs should take a note of this. The invoice was made out by Stransky & Company, New York. The goods were sold to Smith & Ferguson, Limited, Regina, on August 8, 1902. Perhaps before the end of the session the Minister of Customs will get us the information, and we will have the question definitely settled. Now I want to make a reference to my conduct with regard to this affidavit. My hon. friend repeated several times, in face of my specific statement to the contrary, that I refused to give the documents to the House.
So you did.
I say here again that I did not refuse to give the documents to the House.
I leave it to the judgment of the House.

My hon. friend stated that the Minister of Customs turned to me, or directed me, to pass these documents over

to my hon. friend, and X said he was mistaken. Now, I will repeat exactly what did occur. When I sat down, after reading the documents, an hon. gentleman on the other side got up and commenced making a statement. After he had said a few words he called attention to the fact that these documents ought to be given to the House. The question of order arose as to whether I should be compelled to give them to the House, and certainly I did sit back for a little while wondering what would happen. I am a new member of the House, and am not well acquainted with the rules. But I understood the Minister of Customs to say to me, in turning towards me, either ' you do not need to ' or 'you had better not,' or something to that effect.
I rise to a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: You claimed the protection of the Chair when he was interrupting you, now let the member for Assiniboia go on.
Then I suppose we will have the same rule applied to both sides of the House ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: State your point of order.
I understood the Minister of Customs to advise me not to give the document to the House.
I rise to a point of order. When I understood the Minister of Customs to call upon the hon. gentleman to lay the documents on the Table, was that correct 1
That is not a point of order, that is a question of fact.

As I was saying, the Minister of Customs turned round and said something to me, advising me, as I understood, not to give the documents to the House. The point of order was discussed for several minutes, and after awhile I arrived at the conclusion myself that, no matter how the point of order was determined, I would give my hon. friends the privilege of reading the documents. I then called across to the Minister of Customs and said 11 have no objection,' or something to that effect, meaning that I would prefer to give them to the House. I say now that I did not refuse to give these documents to the House. My hon. friend says I ought to apologize for this, he says I had insinuated or had contradicted the Minister of Customs. Certainly I did no such thing, and there is no call for me to make an apology in that regard. But I do think that after my hon. friend has slept over this matter himself he will arrive at the conclusion that an apology is due from him to the people of the North-west Territories, at least to the people at Morden, where he addressed that meeting and told the people that a Regina merchant had informed him so and Mr. SCOTT.
so with respect to this dutiable article, when it has now been proved that the Regina merchant told him no such thing.
We now see the consequence of allowing a mode of controverting a statement made by a member of this House by introducing outside evidence, which, we are informed, it is your duty to prevent.
I was interrupted by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell).
I would like to have the ruling of the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The ruling from the Chair is this : When a charge is made against any hon. member of having said anything, if he gets up in his place and says that he did not make such a statement the hon. member who makes the charge is bound to accept that, and to allow the matter to drop without argument. That is the rule.
Well, I will wait.until the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) takes this course.
Takes what course ? I do not understand what the hon. gentleman means.
Mr. Chairman
I understand that
Mr. Chairman

I am certainly willing to follow the course which has been indicated as being the proper one to follow, but the hon. member for Peel has not denied the statement made in this House that he stated to the people of Morden that a Regina merchant told him so and so. He has not made any denial that he made such a statement.

That is precisely what the hon. member for Peel has said, and now the hon. member for West Assiniboia is going on for the second time to introduce into this House evidence derived from parties outside of this House to controvert what the hon. member for Peel has said. He is entirely out of order, and lie has been ruled out of order on two occasions.
I have not understood it so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Let me state it again. If an hon. gentleman charges another hon. member with having said this, that, or the other thing, on a certain occasion, and if the hon. member says that he did not say that which is charged, then, the hon. gentleman making the statement must accept that from the hon. gentleman who denies it, and the debate then and there ceases on the subject.

I quite understand that. What I was pointing out was that the hon. member for Peel had not denied it, and therefore, I was not called upon to say

anything further on that phase of the subject. Just a word about the question of preferential duties. Many hon. gentlemen -whether the hon. member for Peel did so or not-have gone up and down the country and throughout the length and breadth of the North-west Territories condemning the British preference largely because a merchant in Regina had told the hon. member for Peel that he had brought in certain German goods that had got the advantage of the British preference. I have proved to-night, and I think the proof has been submitted to this committee that the hon. member for Peel was mistaken in regard to that. I believe that all my hon. friends on the other side of the House are just as much mistaken in a great many of the assertions and very much of the condemnation they make on the subject of the British preference.

Mr. Chairman, I am about to pour some oil on the troubled waters. I ask you, Sir, to bring this committee back to the question under discussion. We have not had the question before the chair discussed within the last hour. That is my opinion ; of course, I may not be right, but I think I am right. It is your duty, Sir, to see that personalities are net discussed in this House. I regret to say that we have had nothing but persoualities since the committee resumed after recess, and that the debate has taken this form not only to-day, but yesterday as well. It appears to me that this House is getting to be a beer garden, or is getting as near to it as it	possible for it to get; in fact it
hasa^h a tempest about a teapot. It is about time that we discussed the questions that come before the House in a proper manner. Yesterday we washed all the dirty linen from Montreal and Quebec, and today we have to wash the dirty linen that comes from the North-west Territories and Manitoba.
It is costing $28 a minute.

We have had the razor question discussed, and some hou. gentlemen who are participating in this discussion look as though they never saw a razor. They might have been right on that matter, but whether they are right or not, I am sure they are not right in introducing personalities in this House. Therefore, I call upon you as chairman of this committee, to confine the debate to the question before the Chair, and not to permit personalities to be indulged in. I hope that the time of the House will not be further wasted in the way in which it has been wasted during the last two days.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish, of course, to allude to what has passed, further than to state that there has been a misapprehension,
and I simply allude to it because I do not think any hon. gentleman desires to put any other hon. gentleman in a wrong position. As far as I understand the matter, the hon. member for Peel states that he heard me saying to the hon. member for West Assiniboia to lay the papers on the Table. He heard me saying that, he said, and he judged from that that there had been a reluctance on the part of my hon. friend to do that.
No, no.

I will explain how that happened. Prior to that, when the discussion was going on as to what was incumbent upon a private member, I had said to my hon. friend (Mr. Scott) : You are not compelled to hand the papers to the hon. gentleman. Then, there was a little rest, and my hon. friend, speaking to me, said :	I have no objection to giving the
papers out. Then I said:	You can lay
them on the Table. That is why the hon. member for Peel, hearing that from me alone, and not hearing what my hon. friend had said to me, thought that it was through some instructions to him and not through any willingness on his part that he did it. I simply mention that.
I wish to tell the hon. minister that that was not my understanding of it at all.

In view of the fact that it was through no unwillingness on his part, I thought it was only right that I should say that it was in view of his statement to me : ' I have no objection,' or words to that effect, to give them the papers, that I said :	Then you can lay
them on the Table.
I am sure the hon. minister would not wish to misquote me.
No.

Will you allow me to say this ? I called to the Chair and said: Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) lay the papers on the Table, or send them across the floor of the House to me-and he refused to do it.
No, no.
Well there was a chorus of 'don't do it' from the other side of the House.
That does not prove that he refused to do it.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) wished to make it appear that he was always willing to lay the papers on the Table of the House. It was because he was unwilling that the question came up for discussion at all. I made the statement that we were to thank the hon. Minister of Customs for the papers being laid on the Table, because he turned around and said

to the hon. member for Assinibola :	' Lay
them on the Table.' When the hon. member for West Assinibola got up he said that the hon. Minister of Customs did not make any such statement to him at all.

That is just where the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) is mistaken in what passed between us. But we come now to the question which is an important question, as to the introduction of goods under the preferential tariff. The committee will understand, and business men especially will understand, that it is a very difficult matter under the preferential arrangement to prevent frauds being perpetrated in the bringing in of goods. But I think the House will agree that there is a great deal said in reference to this, that, when it is traced out, as we have had to trace it out in many cases, is found to be without substantial foundation. Without any offence to the hon. member for Peel, let me point out just in this case ; I have no doubt that he thought that the German article which he exhibited came in under the preferential tariff, and that it had been manufactured in Germany.
I made no such statement. What I said was that it was a sample of German goods such as were coming into this country under the guise of the British preference.
I understood that it had been made as an illustration of an article that had come in under the British preference.
I never made such a statement.

I thought the reason that it was exhibited was that it was an illustration that that article had come in under the preferential tariff. I do not say that no articles come in, but this article could not have come in, in such a way. If the statement of the merchant is true that it came from New York in an iron bound case to the port of Montreal where we have our sharp appraisers, then it could not come in except under the general tariff. I will examine into it, but I feel positive that that article could have come in in no other way than under the general tariff.
I cannot conceive it possible that in a port like Montreal these goods could have come in an iron bound ease with * Germany ' stamped on it, and the goods themselves being stamped ' German,' and passed our appraisers there. I am not arguing that there are no goods that so come in. We require the exporter to declare that he is a member of the firm or one who is cognizant of the facts to which he subscribes, and we have not been able to find many houses that would be so careless of their reputation as to make a false declaration.

Has the minister found any goods coming in in the manner in which he Mr. BLAIN.
has described that it was possible for them to come in ?

I think that there have been cases before the department where the question arose as to whether there was the amount of British labour upon the goods that entitled them to the preference, but I have not in mind now any case where such goods came in. I can say that there were no goods solely of German manufacture that came in under the preference.
I never said that.

Nor any that were below the limit. There may have been differences of opinion as to certain goods, but there have been exceedingly few cases. If they were below the limit and we knew it we would put on the full duty. Now the German surtax does not affect the preference at all. It only does this : that now, if German goods have 50 per cent of the value created in Germany they not only pay the general tariff but they pay the surtax on top of the general tariff. If there are any members of the committee who are able to give me the benefit of their experience as to any further precautions that can be taken in the regulations under the preferential tariff I will be only too glad to hear them.
These declarations are not what we understand in this country as declarations having the effect of an oath.

No; they are not affidavits. At the commencement of the preferential tariff we requn^ikhot affidavits should be made, but the^^Tjre a great many complaints. In England they cannot go to a justice of the peace and make an affidavit free of charge as we do here ; they have to go to certain parties who charge them three shillings for each affidavit. That seemed to be a tax upon them, and the department came to the conclusion that if a firm would make a false written declaration over their own hand, they would not hesitate to make a false affidavit and therefore we facilitated business by accepting these declarations.

I wish to say a few words in connection with the discussion which has been sprung upon the committee without any notice having been given to my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain). I can assure the hon. gentleman from West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) that I shall avoid indulging in personalities, for I hold that personalities should never be heard in this House ; but I certainly think that my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) has reason to complain that when affidavits were to be introduced attacking his truthfulness no notice was given to him by the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott). When the hon. member for Assiniboia knew he was going to raise such a question in the committee, it

was due to the hon. member for Peel that he should have been notified. It would also be conducive to the better conduct of debates, if when documents are presented to the House all the documents in connection with the matter under discussion should be laid before us. My hon. friend from Peel has declared that there was a telegram connected with these papers which was torn off before they were sent across the floor of the House.
No.
If I am wrong in that I shall be glad to be corrected.

The telegram was certainly torn off before the papers were sent across the floor of this House, but it was really torn off three or four weeks ago. It was either a copy of a telegram from me to Mr. McCuish, of Morden or from Mr. McCuish to myself, and it had no bearing on the matter.

I have no hesitation in accepting the statement of the hon. gentleman, but I must say that these documents bear indubitable evidence in themselves that they are not complete. If an hon. gentleman reads letters in this House in reply to letters sent by him, and if he expects them to receive the credence of honourable men, it is only reasonable to ask that the letters to which these are replies should be included in the correspondence. After all, what statements are contained in these affidavits that cast the slightest discredit upon the accuracy of the assertions made by the hon. member for Peel ? I will not refer to Mr. Trant because the member for Peel has dealt with him, but let us see what are his declarations. The first three paragraphs refer to his attending certain meetings, which are not important to the issue, and then he goes on to declare :
4.	That at each and every of the three meetings mentioned in the paragraph next immediately preceding, the said Mr. Blain said that the British preference then existing was used by manufacturers in Germany to send their goods to Canada as British goods and so defraud the revenue of the Dominion of Canada, and further, he, the said Richard Blain, explained that the said object was attained by the said manufacturers in Germany first having the said goods shipped to England and thence re-shipped to Canada as British goods entitled to the preference given such goods by the law of Canada.
5.	And I believe particularly that at the aforesaid meeting held at Qu'Appelle on the said 27th day of September, A.D. 1902, the said Richard Blain produced a razor which he said he had bought at Regina in the said Territories the day before, and which he said was a razor of German manufacture and had been imported into Canada under the British preference in the manner described in the paragraph next immediately preceding.
6.	And I further say particularly that at the aforesaid meeting held in the evening of the 30th day of September, in the year 1902 at Wa-pella, the said Richard Blain said he had
bought a teapot in Regina that had been made in Germany and that the merchant who had sold him, the said Blain, the said teapot, or the assistant to the said merchant, had at the request of the said Richard Blain shown him the invoice of the goods of which the said teapot formed a part and that the said invoice was as if for goods that were shipped from England and had received the benefit of the British preference.
What does my hou. friend hope to make by reading an affidavit of that kind to the committee ? How does it asperse the character of my hon. friend from Peel for truthfulness, or affect the statements made by him or by others on this side of the House respecting the British preference, and its operation in the past in securing a preference for German goods ? The statement made in this affidavit is quite consistent with what has been said on this side of the House, and reflects accurately what the hon. member for Peel has said here and elsewhere, and what he has stated to-night. The statement is a fact that can be corroborated.
It is not denied by the minister.
Will the hon. gentleman take now the answer to his question ?
Well, what is it ?
The reason I read this affidavit was that the hon. member for Peel said, in answer to a statement which I had already made, that he had only brought up this subject at one point.
I never made such a statement.
That is what I understood the hon. gentleman to say.
What I said was this, that I exhibited a teapot at one meeting only, and that was at Morden.
That was a second statement.
I may be particularly obtuse, but I certainly cannot appreciate what point has been made by the hon. member, for Western Assiniboia by reading this affidavit.
The affidavit showed that the subject was discussed at more than one meeting.
That is not denied. I had occasion to discuss the British preference on many occasions during my trip in the west.
Did you have a teapot ?

I left the teapot witli the hon. member for West Assiniboia and the hon. member for Peel. The hou. gentleman brings into the discussion this affidavit, which does not amount in value, so far as the matter of the teapot is concerned, to the

[DOT]worth of the paper on which it is written, and this other affidavit made by Mr. Mc-Cuish, which I have not been able to read. Then, attached to these documents is a letter from the Smith & Ferguson Company, Limited, hardware merchants, of Regina, signed hy .T. W. Smith, the president of the company. On the second page of the letter is this statement, to which I draw the attention of the committee :
I note also that, as you pointed out, a portion of the press makes the charge that the Regina firm from whom Mr. Blain bought the teapot has been guilty of defrauding the customs, inasmuch as the benefit of the preference could not have been obtained upon such an importation without the making of a false declaration.
I appeal to my hon. friend if it accords with the measure of fair play which he would expect to have dealt out to himself to suggest to this gentleman that a portion of the press had made allegations reflecting upon my hon. friend, without giving the statements made by other portions of the press ? Why should he make suggestions to the gentleman who wrote the letter ?
They were true suggestions.

My hon. friend from Peel has denied them again and again, and surely my hon. friend from West Assiniboia will not repeat them after that denial ? I heard the statements made by my hon. friend from Peel, and there is not a particle of truth in the suggestion that he charged the firm at Regina with fraud.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I do not think anything in thnt letter indicates that the hon. member for Peel charged the firm with fraud. What the letter indicates is that there were certain charges made in a portion of the press against the firm, based on the statement made by the hon. member for Peel.

My hon. friend bases the whole of his argument on the letter which he got from the Messrs. Smith & Ferguson, of Regina, referring to statements made in certain portions of the press and for which he wants to hold the hon. member for Peel responsible. I am sure that in his calm moments he will not regard that as a very strong argument to press against my hon. friend. The hon. gentleman, if he wanted to make this file complete, should have included in it a copy of the letter to which this is a reply. I am sure that if he had written to the members of the firm for the letter, they would willingly have sent it back. In their letter they say :
The fact is, however, that if the fraud were committed, it was not committed by our firm, as the duty upon the consignment of which the teapot was a part was not paid by us at Regina, but was paid by the brokers from whom we purchased this consignment at Montreal.
Now, I do not know' that there is much more for me to say about this matter. I Mr. CLARKE.
am sorry I cannot read the affidavit of Mr. McCuisli; but I have no doubt the hon. member for Assiniboia read it correctly. Now% the hon. Minister of Customs made a statement with regard to this matter which I think w'ill bear investigation. He said that goods manufactured in Germany could not come in under the British preference, unless they wrere enhanced in value to the extent of 25 per cent by British labour. 1-Ie also said it was impossible for these goods to come direct to the port of Montreal and get the advantage of the British preference if they were shipped in the original packages. Where does the hon. minister get his authority for these statements 1 Let me read a paragraph from the circular issued by his department defining and interpreting this regulation, to the customs collectors at Regina, at Winnipeg, at Toronto, and everywhere else throughout the Dominion :
In estimating the labour of the United Kingdom entering into the production of articles manufactured therein partly from imported material, the extent of such labour may be reckoned by the value of the manufactured article ready for shipment at the place of production after deducting therefrom the value on entering within the limits of the United Kingdom, represented hy the component parts of such articles which are the produce of countries not entitled to the benefits of the preferential tariff.
What does that mean ? It means exactly the interpretation put upon it by the hon. member for Peel and by others on this side of the House, that the profits of the importer can be added to the value of the goods brought in from Germany, and these profits are to be accounted and reckoned as British labour. There is no reason why these packages to which the hon. member referred, if imported into England and valued at $800 should not have been exported thence to Canada at a value of $1,000, and come in under the British preference *, and if that be the case, my hon. friend is vindicated in every statement he made. I took the liberty last year of drawing the attention of the hon. Minister of Customs to a statement made hy one of the most influential papers published in the United Kingdom, describing the way Canada w'as being robbed under this preferential clause, and I shall again quote that statement for the information of the hon. member for West Assiniboia :
How Foreigners Rob Canada.
Since Canada granted a preference tariff to Britain, tons upon tons of German and foreign textiles have been brought over to England and reshipped to Canada after the so called process of ' finishing.'
My hon. friend from Peel has explained how this is done.
In order that they may be classed as goods partly of British manufacture. In some cases this ' finishing1 in England consists simply in taking off the German and French or Austrian labels, doing the goods up again and then giv-

ing them a British name or label. There is not a branch of trade in which this stj-le of smuggling is carried on to the extent that it is in the textile trade.
Has any hon. gentleman any doubt as to what that means ? Will any one hesitate putting faith in that statement which I have taken from one of the most influential papers published in the United Kingdom, the Belfast * News ' ? If the hon. member for Assiniboia has any doubts, he can look up the files of that newspaper and see for himself whether I have not quoted exactly what it said. That statement may be further proven by the circular letter which the hon. Minister of Customs issued to his officers throughout all the customs districts, instructing them how they are to interpret this preference. That being the case, can there be any doubt entertained by hon. gentlemen opposite as to the effect of this preference, and is not my hon. friend from Peel amply sustained in every statement he made with reference to its operation, at every meeting which he had the pleasure and the privilege of addressing in Manitoba and the North-west? My hon. friend from Assiniboia has been always a great stickler for this British preference and has continually appealed to the people of the west to support the government because it had reduced the cost of the goods which they consumed which were imported under this clause of our tariff. Yet, as my hon. friend from Peel pointed out in the course of a recent debate, the hon. member for Assiniboia had not a word to say when the government introduced the surtax, which cannot fail to destroy the effect of this preference on the large importations of goods brought into England from Germany and thence exported into Canada. As the hon. gentleman and the Minister of Finance well know, that is what the surtax will do. What are the provisions of this surtax :
Articles which are the growth, produce or manufacture of any foreign country which treats imports from Canada less favourably than those from other countries may be subject to a surtax over and above the duties of schedule A, such surtax in every case to be one-third of the duty as fixed by such schedule A.
Such surtax shall apply to any article, the chief value of which was produced in such foreign country, although it may have been improved or advanced in value by the labour of another country, notwithstanding the provisions of the British preferential tariff and regulations thereunder.
What is the effect of this enactment ? I will let the bon. Minister of Finance answer that question. Two years ago, I asked the government its intention in regard to barring out goods partly manufactured in Germany, or manufactured from raw materials grown or produced in Germany, from the advantage of the British preference clause, and the Minister of Finance replied :
In answer to the question of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) I beg to say : No. Such provision would practically destroy the British preference inasmuch as British manufactures are largely produced from foreign raw materials.
I do not intend to take up the time of the committee at greater length. I congratulate the hon. member for Assiniboia on any political capital or advantage he has gained from this discussion, and the hon. gentleman who is leading the House (Hon. Mr. Fielding) and the hon. Minister of Customs on this additional evidence of their desire to transact, as expeditiously as possible, the business before parliament.

As the bon. member for West Assiniboia has spoken to-night with regard to the preferential tariff and bow it works, I wish now to call the attention of my bon. friend the Minister of Customs to the fact that the customs regulations make it possible for goods to be imported Id Canada under the preference, which were finished in England, without any regard as to what value had beeu added to these goods by the finishing process. I would call the attention of the minister to bis own regulations-and to the manner in which they have been carried out. Here is the affidavit to be made both by the importer and the exporter.
That the said goods are properly described in the said invoice ; that there is included as specified in the said invoice the true value of all cartons, cases, crates, boxes and coverings of any kind and all charges and expenses incident to placing said goods in condition packed ready for shipment to Canada.
What does that mean ? It means that the values of all cases, coverings, crates, &c., on which there is not duty at all, may be Included in the value. It means that the labelling of the goods and everything else, whether meaningless or not, whether It adds to the value or not, may be included in order to give the appearance of twenty-five per cent of British work having been added, and thus entitle the goods to come in under the preference. The ingenuity of the trade will always take advantage of that, and I have no hesitation in saying that these regulations are open to the greatest possibilities of fraud on the revenue. I do not propose at this stage to continue the discussion and would not have said anything if the bon. Minister of Customs had not made some references himself to this point.

As there has been oil poured on the troubled waters, I propose now to move that the committee do rise, in order that I may discuss the ru'ing which you, Mr. Chairman, made a short time ago with reference to my right of appeal from your ruling to the Speaker. I wish to draw the attention of the Postmaster General,

who is a lawyer and an old member of this House, and also-and especially-the attention of the Finance Minister, to this point.
I said that in all cases there was an appeal from the Chairman of the Committee of the Whole, to the House. I was ruled out of order by you, Sir, and you quoted in support of your ruling clause 70 of the Orders of the House :
Questions of order arising in the Committee of the Whole House shall be decided by the Chairman, subject to an appeal to the House.
I, unfortunately, said that the appeal was to the Speaker. I had seen it a dozen times in this House, yea, twenty times, when the Chairman's ruling was objected to, the Chairman, perhaps, as on the present occasion, may have been at dinner, but he was called instantly from dinner and brought into the House for the purpose of deciding the question. I was overruled by you in the Chair, and you decided that there was no appeal to the Speaker in the Chair. I would like to know what the meaning of the rule is ' subject to the appeal of the House ? ' Does not the House mean the House sitting with the Speaker in the Chair ? In confirmation of my interpretation of the point, let me draw to your attention the authority whom you quoted to prove that my contention was entirely wrong, and you will see that the quotation I make applies exactly to the question now under debate:
Questions of order arising in Committee of the Whole House shall be decided by the Chairman subject to appeal to the House, but disorder in the committee can only be censured by the House on receiving a report thereof.
Now, writing in reference to that rule, Bourinot says :
The first case of appeal to the House under this rule occurred in the session of 1885, but it has its grave inconveniences, since the House is called upon suddenly and without debate to decide a question of order which many of its members may not have heard discussed in committee and the result is, in the majority of cases, a political vote. Under all the circumstances the committee should hesitate before resorting to such an extreme measure. In such a case, it is for the Chairman of the committee to report in writing the point of order which he has decided, and the Speaker must then submit the matter to^the House in the language reported to him, and put the question, ' That the decision of the Chairman be confirmed.'
And be goes on :
If it be found expedient in either House to refer a point of order to the Speaker, a member will move that the Chairman report progress and ask leave to sit again that day. When the Speaker has resumed, the Chairman will report that the committee wishes to be instructed as to the point in question. The House will then proceed to take the matter into consideration, and the Speaker having been requested to give his opinion will decide the matter in dispute ; then unless there is an appeal to the House against the Speaker's decision, the committee will resume its proceedings.

Now, I wisli to draw your attention, again Mr. Chairman, to my interpretation of the rules of the House, supported by Bouri-not's remarks upou the procedure ; and I have no doubt that, upou further consideration of the question, and, after consultation with the Speaker, if you will be kind enough to ask his opinion, there will be no occasion for an lion, member again to be overruled in this committee on this point, for I think that the authority I have given clearly confirms my view and establishes it as the correct one in the premises. As this is a question of privilege, and a grave one, I would like to hear the government's opinion upon it.

I thought my hon. friend from South Lanark had accepted the suggestion that, as we had passed from the point then in discussion and taken up other matters, this question should be left in abeyance. He is aware that it is too late to make a formal appeal, because nless it is taken at the moment that the question arises, we are likely to be confused as to the precise point. I confess that, at the moment, with other matters that have been discussed, I have some difficulty in appreciating exactly what was the point which arose. At all events, he could not now take appeal against the decision. I think his own suggestion is a good one, that you, Mr. Chairman, might look into the matter and consider the point more at your leisure.

This, I understand, is not brought forward for the purpose of making a formal appeal. But, as I understand you, Mr. Chairman, your decision was that in such a case as arose, the appeal was to the committee. Of course, we do not expect any chairman to be infallible in giving decisions, as he is called upou to give them, at short notice. But I think it is perfectly proper and highly judicious for the hon. member for South Lanark to call the attention of the Chairman to the rule and its interpretation showing that the appeal in such a case is, apparently, not to the committee, ns I understood you to say, but to the House, the Speaker being called for that purpose.

As 1 understood the point under discussion with the hon. member for South Lanark, it was as to whether the Speaker was bound to give an opinion. It would appear that, under the rule, the Speaker would decide nothing himself but would submit the case to the House.
I beg the hon. minister's pardon, the Speaker decides the point, and then if necessary, there is an appeal to the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
My view of the rule is just as I put it and that is my view of the rule still-that the Speaker does

not decide the question, but that the appeal is to the House.

How can the Chairman hold that opinion in view of the rule that the hon. member for Soutli Lanark has just read ? It is an appeal to the House, but the House is not constituted until the Speaker is in the Chair.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The rule says :
Questions of order arising in Committee of the Whole House shall be decided by the Chairman, subject to an appeal to the House.
I would understand that to be an appeal not to the Speaker, but to the House, the Speaker putting the question to the House as it has been conveyed to him. I think my interpretation is perfectly correct.
I trust, Mr. Chairman, you will take the matter into consideration and will consult the Speaker. And, perhaps, at a later day, you may revise your opinion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am not of opinion that my interpretation is wrong.
Oh, well, you are altogether wrong.

I understood, Mr. Chairman, that the rule you laid down, perhaps inadvertently, was that the appeal was to the committee. It seems quite apparent, from the rule and the interpretation by Bourinot, that the appeal is to the House constituted by the Speaker taking the Chair.
I withdraw the motion that the committee rise.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We can get a decision again. I am perfectly satisfied, on looking into it that my decision is in accordance with the rule.
Shall this item be adopted ?

What item, Mr. Chairman ?
Mr. DEPUTY- SPEAKER. Now, I want the committee to rule just here. When the committee decided to consider this matter item by item, did they intend that I was to keep the speakers to the consideration of the question in each item ? The committee fails to support me when I try to keep the discussion within the proper limits. Now, I want to know just here if it is the will of the committee to discuss each of these items separately ? If that be so, then the speeches must relate to each one separately. If it is understood by the committee that there is to be a general discussion upon the whole Bill, then I will know what to expect.

The opinion of the committee should not govern you at all, Mr. Chairman. The rules of the House and the proceedings laid down in such cases should
be your guide. Never mind what the opinion of the committee is, because it would be impossible to know what it was at every moment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: 1 must differ with my hon. friend there, because the rules say that when a resolution consists of a number of items, it is for the committee to decide whether the resolution shall be discussed as a whole or item by item. But. if the committee decide to discuss the resolution item by item, then they are to be restrained from going outside the particular item under discussion.

The direction is positive that whether the resolution is discussed item by item or in the whole, the Chairman must be guided by the rules of the House of Commons, independent of the feeling of the committee of the moment.
We had better keep the discussion to each item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are on item No. 2, about the composition of the board.
I presume a Bill wall be found upon this resolution ?
Yes.

Unless the government are prepared to communicate their intention, to say what they mean by making a change in the composition of the board of customs, which is a difficult thing for them to do in the absence of a Bill, I do not see that we could discuss this section at the present time.
Before we assent to the resolution, we should understand what they mean. I think the Minister of Customs should now explain why he is seeking this cha nge.

The intention is that the board of customs shall comprise in the future the commissioner of customs as chairman, and such other officers in the service as shall be designated or appointed by Order in Council. At present the board has upon it members from Vancouver to Halifax, and it is not convenient to summon them at all times when it may be desirable to have a meeting. It is really to get over that difficulty as much as anything else, that we propose this change. The powers of the board will be the same as before. Many members of the present board will, no doubt, continue to act in that capacity.
Who are the members of the board in Montreal?

Mr. Brossard is one, the hardware appraiser, Mr. Douglas, is one, and Mr. Andrews. Mr. Thompson, of Hamilton, is on it. the hardware appraiser in Toronto is on it. These

gentlemen generally attend here. I do not know that we would call the appraisers from Vancouver or Halifax. In a'dditiou to those I have mentioned, are Mr. McMichael, the chief inspector, Mr. Breaduer, of the inside department, and Mr. Woods, another gentleman in the department.
What are the duties of the assistant commissioner of customs to be ?

It is stated in the Bill that he shall perform such duties as the Governor in Council aud the minister may assign to him. Of course he will take the position of chairman, if the commissioner of customs is absent.

Is it the intention of the department to divide up the duties of the commissioner and to allot a portion of them to the assistant commissioner, or is he rather to be regarded as deputy of the commissioner ?
He will only be an assistant. The commissioner will be the deputy head of the department. The assistant commissioner will only be an assistant to the commissioner.
What salary will he have 1
I am asking the House for $2,800. The commissioner gets $3,000.

Three or four days ago I got a letter complaining of the way in which duties are collected on salt. I was given to understand that the amendments are not followed in Hamilton as they are in Montreal. If I remember right, I was told that in some ports they charge a duty on the bags and not in other ports. Would that matter fall under the control of the board ?

That would be a matter for the department to arrange, we should attend to that ourselves. There are complaints once in a while, aud . they are always looked into and rectified. We have to have a uniform rule. If it is stated at any port that they do not understand a rule in the same way as at other ports, a ruling goes out from the department to make the custom uniform. If a new article of commerce comes in which is not specifically mentioned in the tariff, and there is a question under what head it comes, then the board gives a decision. As I said before, when they arrive at a decision it is submitted to the minister, and when the minister signs it it has the force of law, except that there is an appeal to the Governor in Council.
Is not the minister mistaken in regard to the salary of the commissioner of customs ? I understood it was only $2,800.

It was $2,800, then he got $800 as chairman of the board of customs. In the east this year I did not think it desirable to have it divided and I think the committee have already endorsed the recommendation that ft be fixed at $3,600, the same as it has been in the past only it was put under two different heads. I saw no reason for that. I thought it looked better and that the commissioner was worthy of having his salary stated at $3,600. I am free to confess he is a cheap man at that money.

When the item in regard to the assistant commissioner was run through the committee I think the hon. minister then stated that in many instances he would take the place of the commissioner. In such a case does the assistant commissioner receive anything above the salary voted to him as chairman of the board of customs when he acts as such ?

No, it would be an exceptional circumstance that we should call a meeting of the board of customs during the absence of the commissioner. I do not recall anything that would occur to lead us to call a meeting of the board of customs when the commissioner of customs was away. I should want the commissioner to be there because it is important, and if he did preside he would not get any extra salary.

In answer to the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) I understood the hon. Minister of Customs to say that the work of the assistant commissioner would be confined to performing the duties of the commissioner in his absence and of assisting him generally. If that is his duty it seems to me that the salary of $2,800 is rather a heavy salary to pay such an officer as that. It seems to me that for a much smaller amount you could get a man whose duties are simply those of a deputy.

That amount was determined upon because when, a few years ago, we had an assistant commissioner, that was the salary that was paid. When you remember that at some of our ports the collectors get $4,000, that the commissioner who is over the whole Dominion gets only $3,600, and that the assistant commissioner, who, in his absence will have to do his work, gets only $2,800, it will be seen that their salaries are not excessive.
A collector has large financial responsibility.
The collector for the port of Lunenburg does not get the salary mentioned by the hon. minister. He is doing more work than any collector in the province of Nova Scotia.
No, he does not get $4,000.
The salary is so small that the man can hardly manage to live, and he is doing more work than any two, or three other collectors in the province.
Perhaps it should be increased.

We are asking the hon. minister if he will not increase this collector's salary.
On section 3,
In employing temporary officers in the customs do they pass a civil service examination ?

Not necessarily. If they become permanent officers they would have to pass the civil service examination save and except in one position; that is that of preventive officer, which is not required under the law.

If, in view of the enormous business which is being done in the customs' houses all over the country, it is necessary at all to employ a man or men I think it would be necessary to employ them permanently. I think these temporary officers are expensive and inefficient, and that by the time they become efficient they get other employment, whereas, if you required them to pass a civil service examination and put them on the permanent list you would be much more likely to get good men.

I quite agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock). We have what are called temporary officers who have been eight, twelve or fifteen years in the employment of the department and I would like to have them all on the permanent list if they could pass the qualifying examination. But, they are men who are up in years, who were appointed many years ago, and who could not pass the civil service examination. They could have passed) it when they first left school. I have no doubt but they would hesitate to undertake it now and for that reason they are retained as temporary officers. In some cases we have appointed them to the only position we could without their passing the civil service examination, and that is to the position of preventive officer-but we like them to pass the examination in every ease when they can.
There is one point I want to explain and it is that no officer over thirty-five years of age can apply for examination under the Act. He must be thirty-five years of age.
That is in the inside service.

How many temporary officers has the hon. gentleman ? He seems
to be asking for authority to appoint temporary officers. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman has in the service what may be termed temporary officers.
That is in the outside service.

I quite understand that. In the outside service no examination is passed by persons who may be collectors or preventive officers. The hon. gentleman does not exact of those whom he makes collectors of customs that they shall pass an examination. I am not finding fault with the character of those who have been appointed, I believe they are efficient officers, but there are men of advanced years who could not pass the examination. In fact I believe it has not been the rule.
Collectors of customs have not under the law to pass the civil service examination.
Nor preventive officers ?

Nor preventive officers. Appraisers pass a technical examination. You can understand that a man who has to value goods must undergo a technical examination, which takes place under forms set by the commissioner of customs. I cannot tell the hon. gentleman* how many temporary officers we have, but we have a very large number in different places and some of them have been ten or twelve years or more in the service.
The hon. gentleman wants authority to make them permanent officers in the outside service. Is that the power the hon. gentleman is asking for here 1

No. We have been appointing temporary officers, as all governments have been doing. You could not work the department unless there was power to appoint temporary officers at times, because the need arises very suddenly. A man is placed on the temporary list to do the work that is required of him. We thought that the Act would be made clearer in reference to the appointment of them if the power to appoint these temporary officers was specifically placed in the Act. It has been done ever since confederation, it has been recognized as an absolute necessity and we are now just simply making it clear that the law gives its sanction to such appointments.

Does the hon. gentleman propose to increase the number of temporary officers or do I understand that he simply wants to put himself right by taking power to do what he is at present doing but without authority or law ?
Yes.

Speaking of those temporary officers, while I know they cannot be made permanent under the Civil Service Act, yet at the same time steps should be taken with a view of placing them on a permanent footing in the service. There are a number of excellent officers in the customs service, and although many of them were appointed years and years ago and have continued in the employment of the government until they are passed doing anything else in life, yet they still remain In a temporary position. I do not mean to say that they should be given the annual increase in salary, but there should be some understanding that they are permanent officials. For instance, the present government have made a number of these appointments, and should a change of government take place these officials always feel uncertain as to their position. I believe that civil servants who have faithfully discharged their duties should not be subject to such a contingency. I believe they should be free from the whims of any political party and the government should consider some means of protecting that class of employees.
There is a great deal in what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) says, but the Civil Service Act stands in the way.
Is there no way of getting over it; surely the Act could be amended.
Is there any fixed scale of salary for the temporary officers in the employ of the government ?

There is no fixed scale, but there will be a provision .in the Bill that we shall not appoint temporary officers at higher salaries than permanent employees receive in the rank to which they are appointed. The statutory increase does not apply to the outside service. Applications for increases of salary come in, and we have to give our best consideration to them. Under existing circumstances I think myself that we have officers in our employ who are not receiving ample compensation, and that is one of the reasons why I will ask the House for a larger vote for next year.
On section 4,
Is the kon. gentleman seeking by this clause to enlarge the power of the board, or is it to define existing powers that are considered uncertain ?

When the Board of Customs makes a ruling, that ruling has the force of law wtoeu signed by the minister. Suppose a ruling is given that an article should be only 20 per cent on which 30 per cent had previously been charged at different ports, then the parties could make claims on the department, or if Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
the regulations were vice versa, the department would call upon the parties to make amended entries running back two or three years. This is to define that when a ruling of the Board of Customs is given, it takes effect at once and that there shall be no claim for refunds by the parties who have paid too much, or no claim by the government on the parties who may have paid too little.

Is not that unfair ? The customs officers through the country have the matter very much in their own hands, and the importers must pay such duties as are exacted. I should think that under the ordinary working of the Customs Act the cases would be rare in which the importer paid too little, because before he could get his goods he has to submit to whatever ruling the departmental officers may make.	It
seems unfair that in case a mistake was made the importer should have no means of recovering the excessive amount which lib paid.

It
might have that appearance on the face of it, but we have given this matter a good deal of consideration and I think the hon. gentleman will see that it is not so unfair as he thinks. If we said that we would not let them come upon us for refunds, but that we would call upon them to pay if the rate charged was too low, that would be unfair. But the rule works both ways and there will not be many cases in which the Board of Customs will give rulings contrary to what has been the usual practice ; although exceptional cases may occur. Suppose the Board of Customs should rule that the duty should have been 30 per cent when only 20 per cent was paid, and the department was to ask all the merchants to pay the extra 10 per cent, their reply Would be that they only charged for their goods on the basis of a 20 per cent duty and that the department was in effect taking the money out of their pockets. On the other hand, if they have paid too high a rate of duty they would have put that duty on their goods when they were selling them and these goods would have been sold in all probability on the basis of the merchant having paid 30 per cent duty.

It does not change the nature of the grievance that the extra tax has been paid by the customers of the importer, rather than by the importer himself. The hon. gentleman is now imposing a burden upon persons who are entirely innocent, because they were subject to the rulings of his own department and they had no alternative but to submit to the mistake of the customs officers. Some cases may arise where it is not possible to have a general rule on the matter, but so far as it is possible we should not punish innocent persons for mistakes made by the customs officials. I do not think the hon. gentleman should

have such a law. Nobody should be made to suffer for inaccuracies committed in the Customs Department, without having an opportunity for redress.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) The rule is that when a person goes to a customs office to pass his entry, if there is any doubt about the duty to be paid, the article is sent to the appraiser to decide what the duty will be.
Is he an expert ?

Yes, there are expert appraisers on hardware, medicines and everything else. In case the duty paid has been less than it should be, the merchant is asked to amend his entry; but if the duty paid has been more than it should be, an appeal is made to Ottawa and the excess is refunded to him. This has been the practice in Halifax, where I was collector of customs for fourteen years, till the Tories turned me out.

Suppose a man pays too high a percentage of duty, and no reference is made to it at the time, and it is not discovered for a long time afterwards, say six months. There may be many cases of that kind arising in which there is great room for hardship, and I think they should not have effect given them by an Act of parliament.
In most instances there is too little duty paid rather than too much.
I would like to know from the Minister of Customs what the meaning of the legislation is that he proposes to found on these resolutions.

I thought I had explained it already. What the hon. member for Victoria has said is correct, and covers the greater part of the question. If the rate charged has been too much, the case comes to Ottawa, and a refund is paid to the importer. If, on the other hand, it is discovered in the check branch that he has paid too low a rate, then he is required to make an amended entry and pay the balance. These cover the great bulk of the transactions. What this clause refers to is a case that may come before the board of customs. Such cases, however, will be very few and far between. These are cases in which there has been a certain ruling for a length of time, but when attention is called to it, the board of customs decide that the ruling has not been correct, and they lay down a correct ruling. In such cases no claims should come from parties who have paid too much nor any charge made against parties who have paid too little.

That is not the class of cases I call attention to. Suppose an importer pays say 30 per cent duty through the mistake of a collector when he should 98
have paid 20 per cent. He makes no complaint or protest at the time, but six months later he discovers that he paid too much. How would the hon. gentleman deal with a case of that kind under the authority he is now asking to close the door ?

If it is not a decision rendered by the board of customs his claim would be considered and he would get his refund. Suppose three or four or six months have elapsed. It is true, we may have taken money that we should not have taken, but that has not been a burden on the importer. The extra duty has gone into the price which the consumers have paid for the article, and it would be practically impossible to refund the excess to them. The importer has not lost anything as an individual. In these rare cases we do not propose to pay anything on the one hand or take anything on the other. If the hon. gentleman will think the matter over until the Bill is introduced, and still sees the objection he now refers to, we will discuss it further with him.
I want to ask one thing more. It seems to be the object of this legislation that the department will not be compelled to exact payment in such cases ?
Yes.

In another case, suppose you have charged too little duty, say 20 per cent when you should have charged 30 per cent, and the goods have been disposed of. It would be a great injustice to the merchant then to demand the additional duty because of a mistake having been made by the collector of customs.
Quite so, and, if this clause passes, we should not be compelled to ask the man for the extra 10 per cent.

That I think would be very fair.
On section 5,
Will that not lead to complication ? There are many cases in which some of these officers would not be able to convert the foreign currency into our currency.

They have tables for that. If goods are made say in Belgium, and purchased in Germany, the present law requires that the invoice shall be made out in the German currency. We are going to allow such invoices to be made out in Belgian currency.
What does the hon. minister mean by ' further particulars shall be given in the invoices.'
That will be more definitely explained in the Bill. I think it is to see that packages and other particulars are sufficiently mentioned in the invoice.
I hope the hon. minister will see that there are no more complications than at present.

This is to secure uniformity as much as possible in the invoices, and to give us sufficient information to know at once how that each invoice can be dealt with.
On section 6,

Suppose an article is made of different components. Suppose, for instance, it is made partly of iron and partly of brass, and there is a duty on the iron machinery of 25 per cent, and on the brass of 30 per cent. If only a small portion of the article is brass it will come in at the 25 per cent duty, whereas under the present it would have to be charged the higher rate.
Does this apply to that section of the Customs' Act which imposes a duty on unenumerated articles of 20 per cent. Or is the hon. minister making two classes of unenumerated articles ?

The unenumerated articles which are charged 20 per cent, are articles that can come under no other definition, but there are certain articles which are not of this class, but which are composed of different component parts, each of which may be subject to a different duty.

I would suggest to the hon. minister to find some other name for the latter than that of 'unenumerated articles ' or he will be confounding them with the unenumerated articles which are charged a duty of 20 per cent.

The Bill itself clearly explains the difference, and I do not think that there will be any confusion. The unenumerated articles referred to in this clause would be manufactured articles composed of two or more materials. For instance, an article might be composed partly of iron and partly of brass. In that case, it would have to come under one or other of these denominations. That having prevailed in the past the article would have to come in under the highest duty applicable to any of the materials of which it was composed-brass, iron or whatever it might be. Under this, it will come in as I said before, under the rate of duty on the article of which it is most largely composed.

How would the hon. gentleman determine a case of that kind ? It seems to me he is raising a very difficult question. Suppose an article composed of a number of different materials-iron, wood, brass, some silver, some l'ead-how can this be decided with any degree of accuracy by any collector of customs ? I doubt if even a customs board could do it. I would not offer an opinion, but, no doubt, the matter has been studied in the hon. gentleman's Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
department. I believe it was found well to lay down an arbitrary rule covering articles of that kind, it being found impossible to come to a correct conclusion in each case. I am not opposing the hon. gentleman, but it seems to me he is getting into deeper water rather than reaching firm ground.
Suppose an article were composed of 75 per cent of something that was free and the remainder of some article that had a duty of 25 per cent. In that ease, I suppose the whole would come in free.
Well, no, we are not in the habit of letting anything come in free if it is composed of dutiable material.
Of course, the Minister of Customs is proceeding upon the idea of a tariff for revenue. I want to assist him in carrying out his policy.
It is not designed to go so far as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) suggested. The article would be dutiable. But, this is a new idea.
It would come in under 25 per cent as unenumerated.
This supersedes the unenumerated 1
No, it assists it, not supersedes it.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman will tell the committee if he has been actually collecting the duties on the scale he proposes, here, or whether he is proposing a new departure from the arbitrary rule of collecting 25 per cent on these articles as coming within the class of unenumerated.

We are making a new departure, and we think, establishing a fair rule. Suppose that an article is composed one-tenth of a material which is subject to a duty of 30 per cent, and nine-tenths of a material which is dutiable at 30 per cent, it would be hardly fair to charge the whole 30 per cent.
The hon. gentleman is charging 20 per cent now under the unenumerated class.

No, we are charging 30 per cent. These articles do not come in under the unenumerated class. An article is accounted unenumerated only when it cannot be classified under one or other of the headings. Articles composed of iron and brass, for instance, though not specially mentioned, are not counted unenumerated, but would be classed either as manufactures of iron or as manufactures of brass.

On section 7,
To extend the time for the submission for claims for refund, including claims for refund on account of damages.

Claims for refund now are required to be put in within ten days from the date of entry or they are shut out. It is thought that that is too short a time, and we propose to extend it to fourteen days from the date of entry or landing. Sometimes an entry is made even before the goods arrive. In many cases, merchants tell us : When these goods were brought into our warehouse, opened and examined, we found they were damaged, but the ten days had elapsed, and we could not enter a claim for a refund.
On section 8,
That importers may be relieved from the payment of duty on damaged goods abandoned in certain cases.

That is new. If a man has a lot of goods coming in and they are so thoroughly damaged that they are not worth to him the amount of the duty, he may abandon them altogether, in which case ,we shall have the right under the law to take the goods and destroy them, charging the importer no duty.
Would it make any difference how this damage was brought about, whether from fire or from careless handling on ship-board ?
