I think this would cover cases of damage from whatever cause. The hon. gentleman will see that the object of the customs duty is to secure revenue on goods that go into consumption. If goods are damaged so much that the importer would rather abandon them than pay the duty, we would destroy them and they would not go into consumption. The question of damage would be a question for settlement between him and the parties who sent the goods.

Suppose the damage was caused by the transportation company from whom the importer could recover. He would abandon the goods, but he would receive the value of them from the transportation company. In that case, some person ought to pay the duty. If the damage arose in such a way that no person was liable, I could understand that the hon. minister's position would be a fair one, but not if the importer could recover the value of the goods. In that case, if the hon. gentleman proposes to relieve the parties from the payment of duties by their merely abandoning of the goods, he goes too far. If a transportation company damages goods, then they ought to be liable. Suppose a man, through carelessness in handling goods, damages them and they became of no value, would that be a reason for relieving him. if they were damaged through his own act ?

The hon. gentleman must not lose sight of the fact that the revenues we collect are on goods that go into consumption in Canada. If the goods do not go into consumption in Canada then we do not expect the people of Canada to pay anything. For instance, $1,000 worth of goods come into this country and go into a bonded warehouse and remain a year or two, they pay no duty, and they are exported to another country. Now this is what we propose : Here is a quantity of goods that are so damaged that the owner says, I will throw them out, I do not want them at all, I will give them to you instead of paying the duty on them. We take these goods, but we do not put them on the market, we destroy them. Now, these goods would have gone into consumption if they had not been destroyed, but after destroying them a like quantity of goods must come in to replace them. Look at it from the customs standpoint alone, the question of abandoning the goods is a question that may be considered with the transportation companies or others who may have damaged the goods; but so far as our revenue is concerned we only collect revenue on goods that actually go into consumption.

I remember a case with which the hon. gentleman is acquainted. I had paid duty upon goods entered for consumption, they were destroyed and never went into consumption. But the hon. gentleman collected a duty. I know of cases in which he has done it. I know of a case in which he came to this House and asked for a refund, he put an item in the estimates to refund to the person who had suffered a loss of that kind.

The hon. gentleman has mentioned a case which illustrates this. A quantity of goods were destroyed at Montreal. Duty had been paid upon them, and before they got into the merchant's warehouse they were destroyed. They were in our custody. The present Act prevents us from giving him back his money as a refund. If he had not paid the duty we could not do it. If he had not paid the duty, then he would not be called upon to pay the duty, because the goods were not there. But he had paid the duty, the goods were there, and before he got them into his possession they were burned. We had the duty, but the law did not allow us to refund it. That case was one of so much hardship that I put a special item In the estimates to pay him back the money.

I am arguing in the hon. gentleman's proposition that no duty was supposed to be collected unless the goods went into consumption. Suppose a case where the man paid the duty, removed the goods to his own warehouse one hour after the duty was paid he took possession of them, and half a million dollars worth of goods were destroyed and never went into consumption, yet the hon. gentleman

would not think under such conditions of refunding the duty. But he based his argument that no duty is supposed to he collected on goods that do not go into consumption.

The expression ' entering into consumption ' is generally understood to mean taken from the warehouse for that purpose. Once the goods are on the shelves of the merchant, I do not see how you can follow them there. The line has to be drawn somewhere, and the line is drawn between goods in the warehouse which have not yet entered into consumption, and goods taken out of the warehouse.

In many cases where the goods are partly destroyed or injured, the way in which the customs deals with them is very fair, that is, they appraise the value of these goods and give a rebate equal to the damage that has been done.
That is the case when they are wholly abandoned, we waive the whole duty. We destroy the goods, we do not put them on the market.
That may apply to some kind of goods, say the goods are damaged or wet through, they still may have some value. Do you destroy those goods ?
In that case the owner would not abandon them. We would give a proportion.
Take a case of fruit coming from a long distance which had become entirely decayed and not fit for use. Would the law apply in that case 1

In a case of that kind it would be a fair thing to say to the man, not only must you lose the fruit, but we will make you pay the duty on it, though it may never have entered the customs at all.
9. That the basis of allowance for damage on polished steel and other articles he changed.

The present law says that we shall only allow on an amount damaged over 50 per cent. We change that, and allow for a damage of over 25 per cent, the same as we do on other goods.
On section 10,

This is the clause that covers what the bon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) -alluded to. As the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) has pointed out, after goods have left our possession and gone into the warehouse of the merchant, if they are burned, they are covered -by insurance, while, if the goods are burned in our possession he has to pay the duty and we have no power to give it back to him without coming to parliament,

because the insurance would not cover the goods on the wharf. If they are in the merchant's warehouse, in his possession, then, he has them insured, but if they are destroyed while in our possession before they have reached him and if he has happened to -pay the duty upon them we are powerless to pay him back the duty. We propose to make power, if they are destroyed in our possession, to return the duty.

Iam sure the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) would be able to enlighten the committee in this respect. Suppose goods were damaged by water on the ocean voyage to- such an extent that the importer was ready to abandon the goods rather than pay the duty, and he had them insured against such damage and collected the insurance-that would be just the other case to which the hon. gentleman referred. In that case the duty ought to be paid.

Is it necessary to have an enactment for that purpose ? In case goods are destroyed upon which the duty has been paid in the custody of the customs, is it not a matter of right that -the duties are refunded ?	.
No, we have not that power. We have to ask for a special vote to cover it, but we are taking that power now.
Suppose ten packages valued at $10 a piece were in t-he custody of the customs -and the custom house was burned who would be' responsible ?
They are -at the owner's risk.
Would the government not be responsible ?
No.

The goods are all insured In transit from the time they leave Liverpool until they reach the warehouse. They are actually insured against all accidents from the time they leave Liverpool both on the voyage and while they are in charge of the customs; in fact until they are in the possession of the merchant.
Would they be insured during transit after they had been landed in Canada ?
Yes, they are insured in store, on the wharf and in the warehouse.

In the case referred to by the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) the goods had been landed in the afternoon and that mght before the merchant could transfer them to his warehouse they were destroyed. Therefore. there was no insurance on them

This will be the section of the Bill that will deal . with this matter :

Upon production of satisfactory proof to the Minister of Customs of the actual injury or destruction in whole or in part of any goods by accidental fire, or other casualty, while the same remained in the custody of the officers of the customs in any customs warehouse, or while in transportation in bond from one port of entry to another port of entry in Canada, or, while within the limits of any port of entry and before the same have been landed under the supervision of the officers of the customs, the duties on the whole or the part thereof so proved to he injured or destroyed may be abated or refunded ; provided the claim be made within 14 days after the date of the casualty and that due appraisement be made* of the goods so alleged to be injured, as soon as they can be examined.
The hon. member for Peel asks a auestion as to the responsibility for the loss of the goods themselves. They would be at the merchant's own risk.
Yes, the goods themselves. We are dealing with duties only.

Does it not seem reasonable, when the government take possession of a man's property and retains it for two or three days until the necessary entries have been made, that they should be entirely responsible for those goods ?	1
think they ought to be liable to the individual for the property which they have in their possession.
The government are not warehousemen. Warehousing is a separate matter.
The goods are insured even when they are in .charge of the customs.

What I mean is this; supposing a poor man imports an article worth $10. That article is sent from New York and put in the customs-house at Ottawa to-night, if is in the possession of the customs and the importer cannot receive it. He could not possibly get possession of it and it is burned up to-night. Is it fair that that poor man should lose that article ?
Get it insured.
An hon. member says get it insured. Ninety-nine out of every hundred of these small packages are never insured.
The hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) says they are.
I refer to importations of goods from England or elsewhere.

Here are ten small articles in the customs house, in possession of the government and they are burned up-should not the government be responsible ? Is it right that these ten men should lose all their effects ? Is it not fair that the government, holding these articles, should be responsible for them until the purchasers of them have an opportunity of getting them into their possession ?

If that is true in regard to a small parcel, it would be a matter of principle that would apply equally to large consignments of goods in warehouse. The question is whether the government are to be responsible for the ownership of property simply because it is put in the warehouse, because the principle is the same. I do not see how you could hold the government responsible. The government simply acts as agent in passing these goods through the customs and in collecting the duty.

If goods come in by mail and are lost, I do not think the government is responsible for them.
On section 11,

In this and the next section it will be found that, we are simply taking these from the tariff Act. For convenience, as we are getting this up with a view to the Consolidated Revenue Act. in the revision of the statutes, we are taking from the Tariff Act this and the next clause without change.
On section 13,

What officers does the hon. member propose to vest with that power ? I have had occasion to find that some officers-I do not say customs officers' particularly-are very lax about the way in which they administer an oath. They seem to think that by the person signing a paper and saying : ' This is all right,' that they have done their duty.
That is the way the lawyers do.

No, the lawyers do not do it in that way with all due deference to my hon. friend. There should be some discretion exercised in regard to the officers who are given power to administer oaths. Some officers, and not inferior officers either, are very lax in administering oaths, and if a charge of perjury were laid, the guilty person might escape because of some technical objection. I impress upon the minister that great care should be taken in the selection of officers to whom be given this authority.

At present we have to get an Order in Council to appoint an officer for this purpose and we want to change that so that the Customs Department can of its own action appoint such a person. There will be just as much care exercised by the department as if these officers were appointed by an Order in Council.
This only gives them power to administer oaths in relation to the Customs Act.

Yes

On section 14,

At the present time the railway and steamship companies are charged for the extra service rendered by officers after hours. They have for years protested against that. Their argument is that the officers are there to protect the revenue of Canada and that the revenue of Canada should pay them. Where officers have rendered services outside of the hours between eight o'clock in the morning and six at night, we have charged the railway companies and steamship companies twenty-five cents an hour, and that money has been paid by them to the Receiver General, and it is checked out and paid through the collector of customs to the men who are entitled to it. I have never been able to find a satisfactory answer to the contention of the transportation companies that the government itself should pay its own officers. I might have said to them that you must have your business transacted at certain hours, but it is our duty to facilitate trade and commerce, and it would be unreasonable and out of the question to require them to run their trains between eight in the morning and six at night. They hold that it is our duty to collect our revenue and pay our own servants, and I must say that they appear to have the best of the argument on their side. The hesitancy about undertaking this before, was I suppose, because a minister does not wish to undertake an expenditure which will run into many thousands of dollars, but I have made up my mind to ask the House to sanction an appropriation that will enable us in the future to pay those men who are our servants and who attend to the duties that we require of them. WTe take power under this resolution, however, in cases where we consider that private interests and not public interests are served, to charge the private interests for the service rendered. For instance, if a railway company should ask that we shall have a man at Boston to examine baggage that is coming into Canada so that it may be bonded through, we would look upon that as being a convenience to the railway company and in such a case the railway company would be required to pay for the services of that officer.
Who fixes the salary of an officer at Boston say.
The Customs Department fixes the salary.

I am bound to say that the Customs Department fixes a very small salary for some of these men in view of the arduous duties they have to perforin. The government are bound to have officers on the frontier both day and night, but I do not think that the officers on the boundary experience as much hardship as some of those in the interior of the country. For Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
instance, a pasenger is coming from the state of New York into Ontario, and he may arrive at any hour of the night and the custom officer may be obliged to be on duty. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Michigan Central at St. Thomas contribute something like $25 a month towards the pay of these officers, and to my mind that is a very small amount indeed. If the minster is going to remedy that, he will be doing right. Officers who are called out of their beds to perform duties for the country, should be better paid than they are now.

It was announced some time ago in the newspapers, that baggage coming into this country could only be sent in bond to certain points. For instance, persons coming from Chicago to the town of Smith's Falls, and checking their baggage to that point, find it detained at the border instead of being sent on.

I think the commissioner met the transportation companies a little time ago and discussed this matter with them. They were anxious to have the baggage examined at the frontier as far as possible, but there were certain other points fixed upon to which the goods might be bonded. The trouble arose in this way : Suppose the goods were coming to some place this side of Cobourg, which was not a port of entry ; they could not be bonded further than Cobourg, and they would be held there to be examined. The party, having arrived at his destination, would miss his goods. It was thought most convenient to have them examined at the frontier ; but in some cases it happened that while the goods should be stopped at Cobourg for examination, the railway company might let them pass on to the other point which is not a customs point at all. That was the reason of the arrangement between the commissioner and the railways under which certain points were selected where the goods might be examined.

I notice that in the list there were very few places to which trunks could be consigned. For instance, the town I come from is not in the list, so that a person coming there would have to have his baggage examined at the border, perhaps at midnight.
If the hon. gentleman's goods were not on the same train with himself, they would be sent on the next day.
Is this going to entail the appointment of a very large number of new officers V
I think it will not entail any new appointments, but it will entail a large expenditure.
Will the service become much more expensive than it was before ?
No, I think we can perhaps rearrange it so that it will not cost so much, but it will cost the country a good deal more, because we shall not have the revenue from it.
Has the hon. minister made an estimate of what amount this service will cost us ?
I think altogether it will cost very nearly $70,000, and I am not sure but that I may have to ask for $100,000 for it.

Does the hon. gentleman propose to fix the compensation in each case for the officers of the department doing these additional duties, or does he propose to come down with a general scale so that the House will know what it is paying in each case ? I am not now complaining of the departure the hon. gentleman has made, because I think what he has stated lias been a great hardship, and I see no reason why the change should not be made and the burden shifted to where it belongs, namely, on the companies. But the question is whether the hon. gentleman is taking power to deal with these cases at his own sweet will, or whether he will come down with some fixed scale.

It will not be at my own sweet will, though I suppose it will be pretty much as I wish. I should have to submit it to my colleagues, and obtain an Order in Council. Many years ago an Order in Council was passed, fixing the rate paid by the railway companies at twenty-five cents an hour, and in my judgment that is not too much.
Is that at the boundary line ?

No, wherever an officer is rendering a service. This extra amount is paid to the officer in addition to his salary. Take the port of Montreal, where we have to have men on the wharfs at night. These men get $500 a year, but they may make an extra $60 or $70 by doing extra service at night. The transportation companies now pay these men at the rate of twenty-five cents an hour, so that if we made a rearrangement, the men would go on doing the work they have been doing, but they would be paid by us instead of by the railway companies. We hope that we may be able to reorganize the department so as to economize a little. I do not think that a man who has to put in a day's work from eight a.m. to six p.m. can do his work efficiently if he also does night work, and I think we can reorganize that system and have men go on for certain hours and then be relieved by others.
In the United States, does the state pay for that service ?

I think the United States bear the whole expense
of the collection of their revenue by night and by day.

Where you have a night staff and a day staff, I do not see what necessity there can be for paying men overtime, unless in the exceptional case where a man on either staff happens to be ill and has to be replaced by one taken from the other staff. But the complaint I make has reference to ports of entry, where you have no night men. A man may come from New York state and have his trunk come to this port of entry. What he wants and what the railway company wants is that he should get his trunk immediately on arrival at the station, and have that trunk released by the customs officer. But if a regular man be called out of his bed to perform that service, he should receive extra pay. In the town of my county, that railway company have been paying at the rate of $25 per month for that service, and if the hon. gentleman will rearrange that kind of service and pay the men more money, he will be doing the proper thing.
Section fourteen of this resolution is very far-reaching. It gives the Governor in Council power to reduce the customs duties. At present he has power to remit the duties but not to reduce them.

My hon. colleague the Minister of Finance pointed out in his budget speech that while the Governor General in Council had the power of taking off the duty altogether, he cannot reduce it. There are many cases in which the government might be disposed to reduce the duty in order to help the manufacturers of certain kinds of goods, but would not feel justified in remitting them altogether.

I have no hesitation in saying that this is a most unreasonable proposition. The government have now the power of remitting the duties, but only under certain conditions. They may place certain articles on the free list for certain purposes clearly specified, but without any safeguard- of that kind the hon. gentleman proposes to take the power of reducing these duties and of practically fixing the duties, which this House ought to have the right to do.
I am not taking the power myself.

the government the power to put goods on the free list, which were the composite parts of articles manufactured in this country, the lion. Minister of Trade and Commerce and the hon. gentleman himself protested strongly against the proposition. But his proposition goes a long ways further. It was safeguarded with everything that was possible-certain conditions had to obtain before the minister could act. Now, he opens the gate as widely as he can and asks the right to reduce the duty on any article without asking parliament.

The hon. gentleman is quite wrong. You will observe that this is a paragraph to be appended to section 245 of the Act, and it will be known as subsection ' U.' We have run down the whole alphabet already to and including 'T.' So, you have given the Governor in Council power-not myself-to make regulations for many things, for instance, for slaughtering cattle and grinding corn in bond.
Does the Governor General do it of his own will or by the recommendation of the hon. gentleman and his colleagues.
The Governor in Council must do it.

But does the Governor in Council do it upon his own motion or upon the recommendation of the minister ?
The MINISTER OF, CUSTOMS. The recommendation in these cases probably comes from the Minister of Customs. Of course, it must originate somewhere. Under subsection ' L ' which is now in existence, the Governor in Council has power to transfer to the free list articles imported to be used as material for Canadian manufacture. It is proposed here, with regard to the same class of articles, to allow the Governor in Council, instead of placing the articles on the free list, to reduce the rate of duty.

I do not think it is the same thing at all, I have not seen the section of the Act to which the hon. minister has referred. But I understand that in certain specified eases mentioned in the Act the Governor in Council may transfer articles to the free list, the cases being there specified.

Not
Specified! but classified generally-articles for manufacturing purposes.
But upon what ground and to what extent would the Governor in Council reduce the duty ? It gives large discretionary power.

Not
more than to-day.
A great deal more, The Governor in Council can now place goods on the free list in certain classified instances determined by parliament.
This is the same case, except that he reduce the duty instead of making the articles free.
Yes, but it is intended to increase the classes in which the duty may be reduced.

My hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) has spoken of certain well understood limitations which, he says, will not apply in this case. He has taken up this section fourteen and judges from it alone. But this is a mere draft statement of the substance of the Bill to be introduced. In conformity with the rule respecting measures of this character, these resolutions are first presented in committee. Bift these do not purport to set forth the details which will appear in the Bill. Every restriction which surrounds the placing of goods on the free list will surround the reduction of the duty. Surely, if the Governor in Council may be entrusted as at present, to make a free gift, they may be trusted to do something less than that.

With all deference to the Minister of Finance, I would say that, in one case he is simply making certain goods free, but in the other case he is making a whole tariff. Parliament has fixed the tariff, but, under certain restrictions, has authorized the Minister of Customs or the cabinet, to allow goods to enter free to be used as material for manufacturing. That is a vastly different thing from parliament saying that the duty on a certain class of goods shall be for instance thirty per cent, but giving the government power to say to any particular class of manufacturers : Because we like you or for some other reason, we will let you have these goods at fifteen per cent.

Taking my hon. friend's (Mr. Lancaster's) illustration-at present we can say : Because we like you, or for some other reason (quoting my hon. friend's words) we will let you have these goods, not at a reduced duty, but without any duty.
No, the cases are specified.

My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) is mistaken, there is no change in the specification. The conditions will be the same in both cases. A manufacturer makes a proposition to us to transfer an article to the free list. We may feel that he is not entitled to have the goods free, for that is a great privilege, but that he makes out a fair case why the duty

should be reduced. We simply ask to be allowed to reduce the duty instead of making the goods free. How It can be argued that there is any extension of the power of th'e Governor in Council in this proposal passes my comprehension. If we have the power given us for the reasons specified to make a free gift, surely it is no extension of the power to say that we may give only part.
Suppose you want to increase the duty ?
But that is not proposed.

Surely the bon. Minister of Finance will not contend that that is an answer. He proposes that the government shall have power which should rest with parliament alone, that of fixing the rates of duty. Whether goods should be entered at a lower rate of duty or should be free are two entirely different reasons.
Move it.

No, it may be moved at a hiter stage. What would be the effect of this ? The government have represented to the country that they have taken off some ot the protective duties they complained of, and what have they given in return ? A lower rate of duty on some raw materials coming into the country. Parliament has thought right and has deemed it safe to give authority to the Governor in Council or to the minister, to come more nearly to the case-under certain conditions to make certain articles free of duty. Now, surely, if they give the minister or the Governor in Council-that makes no difference-
It does.

None whatever. If the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Paterson) presented an Order in Council and his Excellency refused to give it his assent he would resign. The hon. gentleman knows that his recommendations are passed-the passing of them is a mere formality. But I hope the parliament will not surrender to any party in this country the right to fix rates of duty. They may go a long way without abuse-I am not certain that it is not without abuse, though I think on the whole it has been- but there is no parallel between this special grant of power to make goods free under certain circumstances and a new departure in the form of legislation giving power to the Governor in Council to fix rates of duty.
If my hon. friend were attacking the right of the Governor in Council, he would touch this question.
I am not doing that at all.

That is where he is illogical. If he were attacking the right of the Governor in Council to deal
With this matter at all, then I could recognize that at least lie was basing his argument upon some principle. Now, it is well understood that the Governor in Council shall not be allowed to increase a tax, and it is not proposed to violate that principle. But suppose a manufacturer opening a new industry comes to us and says, I am using a certain article, and for the encouragement of this industry I would like to have it put on the free list. We say, no, we cannot do that, the duty is a considerable item, we don't want to lose it, and we do not think you have made out a good case. Your industry has already a certain tariff advantage, and if we give you free materials in addition to that, you are getting an undue advantage. But he may say, I cannot carry on my industry on these conditions, can you not give me some concession ? Then the Governor in Council shall have power to say: No, though we will not give you that thing absolutely free, we will give it to you at a lower rate of duty. If parliament is the only body to be entrusted in the one case, it is the only body to be entrusted in the other. Every condition is the same, and if it is wrong to give the Governor in Council power to reduce a duty under these precise conditions, surely it is equally wrong for parliament to give the government power to make the article free. My hon. friend would say to the manufacturer :	No, we
cannot give you that at all. Now we might get a considerable revenue out of that, but by the course proposed by the hon. gentleman we would be obliged to sacrifice the whole revenue and make it free.
You are dealing with au article that may enter into manufacture.
Yes.

Suppose the manufacturer is making a class of goods upon which he has a duty of so much; would the government step in by Order in Council and say : We think the duty is too much, and we are going to pass an Order in Council to reduce it again ?

We have power to-day to ask to make it free, and under the proposed amendment we will take power to say to him :	No, we cannot give you all that advantage, but we will help you by reducing the duty. My hon. friend's objection would oblige us to give him the whole tiling.

No, I say it is too much power to put into the hands of the Governor in Council. In the matter of the tariff, a manufacturer establishes his business ou the understanding that he is going to have so much protection. Then I say in justice to that man no power outside of parliament should be allowed to interfere with that duty, and that interference should only take place at the session of parliament. But if, in the manufacture of his goods, he is using

a certain class of raw material upon which there is a duty, and that is not interfered with by any other manufacturer, then it might be proper to reduce the duty on the raw maternal.
Not on the raw material, but on the material.

What I object to is that when we frame a tariff it ought not to be interfered with by Order in Council. The hon. gentleman spoke about the will of the minister. Suppose you dislike the manufacturer, suppose you want to take him by the throat and say :	Unless you do so and
so we will reduce the duties 1

This is a proposal to reduce the duty on some article, not necessarily raw material, that he is going to use. Now if a man comes and asks us to give him some concession with regard to an article not made in Canada, and where there could be no question as to its affecting any other industry, we will be able to help him, but it might be too much to give him absolute freedom. Instead of that, we reduce the duty, and the hon. gentleman thinks we are enlarging the power of the government. If he will contend that the Governor in Council should not have power to touch the tariff question at all, there is a principle in that. But if a manufacturer desires a certain privilege and we have power to make an article absolutely free, how do we enlarge our power by being able to say to him : No, we won't make it free, but we will lower the duty.

Suppose a manufacturer establishes a business on the idea that he is getting so much protection, and the government, between the sessions of parliament, steps in and passes an Order in Council to reduce the duty on that particular article, which might drive him out of the business. I say that power should only belong to parliament.
We have now the power, every government has had it, to put that article on the free list, though it may have the effect of driving the manufacturer out of business. Where is the difference ?
Yes, and that is what I hold is wrong, making it absolutely free without the consent of parliament.
That is a consistent position, but that is not the position of the hon. member for Botliwell.

Suppose a manufacturer is making a certain class of goods, and he says that his goods have been driven out of the markets by the hon. gentleman, who is a free trader, not giving him adequate protection. The hon. gentleman says he is aiding that manufacturer less by giving him a reduction of duty than by making the arti-Mr. INGRAM.
cle free. That would seem a very rational argument, but in appearance it is all wrong. The hon. gentleman must justify himself When he puts the article on the free list in the public interest. But according to his own theory, if he reduced the duty partially instead of giving him additional protection, how can he argue that he is doing it in the public interest ? This is giving such a power to the hon. minister that we might just as well relieve him of the necessity of coming down to the House and asking the House to fix the duties on any article which may be brought into this country.

I may be obtuse, but I cannot see the force of the hon. gentleman's argument. The procedure in both cases is precisely the same. You can only do this by Order in Council. I do not object to the contention that it means the Minister of Customs, because we pay great respect to his recommendations. It has to be done in the usual way, the minister has to make a report to council, council must pass judgment upon it and the decision must be published in the ' Canada Gazette.' That condition which exists now in respect to placing an article on the free list must continue to exist in respect to reducing the duty.
That is not the point.
I think it is.

I am not quarrelling with the hon. gentleman as to who does it, or the form in which it is done. Our contention is not in respect to the way in which it is brought about. This is going a long way in the direction of giving the government power to legislate by Order in Council, to take certain articles from a fixed duty and place them on the free list. This additional power is going too far and is placing a weapon in the hands of the government that should never be wielded by any government I care not which party may be in power.
We are not asking additional power ; we are asking a lesser power than we have now.
I think the hon. gentleman is asking for a power that he will exercise very much more than he would exercise the present power.

I really do not think so.
Mi-. HENDERSON. Now, the minister at all times requires to have a revenue. He hesitates about placing an article on the free list because he knows he is going to lose the revenue that would accrue from that article. That alone would restrict him very much in the exercise of this extraordinary po'wer which has been placed in the hands of the government for so many years. It is an extraordinary power and

perhaps in that we have made a mistake. It may be desirable to go back the other way, to undo something we have done, but in regard to the partial reduction of duties, the minister may say :	I want
revenue ; here is an article on the list which pays 25 per cent. There is very little of that article coming into the country under a 25 per cent duty ; I will reduce it to 15 per cent to meet the views of this manufacturer and I will get a good deal more revenue out of a 15 per cent duty than. I will out of a 25 per cent duty. Hence, I fear that power, if it were for nothing more than the purpose of getting revenue, may be exercised a great deal more than the present power of putting an article on the free list. The government would have an incentive if they wanted revenue to make these reductions which perhaps would be altogether contrary to the wishes of parliament. There is a strong point in this and I think it is well that it should be thoroughly considered before we embody it in the law.

I agree that the subject is important and before the Bill to be introduced reaches its final stage, there is no reason why it should not be reconsidered. There is no disposition on the part of the government to exercise that power frequently and although the bon. gentleman describes this power as an extraordinary one I think he will find that not only by this government but by all governments it has been used very sparingly, and I am sure it will continue to be used very sparingly and only for good reasons.
